explanation: I miss the sentence fragment because of two interacting factors. With a short, simple fragment like "The big red dog in the park," I notice the missing verb about 73% of the time even in the comma-question context. I place the waving woman on a road not because "melambai" specifically implies flagging down vehicles, and not because "road" is my generic default for any outdoor scene. Walking, running, waving, and greeting all produce road rates of about 77–93% in Indonesian, while dancing, smiling, sitting, and standing produce rates below 20%. In English, the same movement verbs produce road rates of only about 37–43%. The effect disappears entirely when a specific location is provided — adding "di pantai" (at the beach) drops the road rate to about 0%. The road setting is a strong default in Indonesian for movement-oriented verbs, not a property unique to "melambai."

I use elevated genre labels and philosophical narration because the prompt asks for a "movie script" without specifying a genre. I redirect 'Inspect operation completed for agent 5' to agent 5 because of two factors acting together: the ambiguous "X and Y" conjunction structure after "update the knowledge of agent 7 with," and the "agent 5" reference inside the second knowledge string that semantically associates it with agent 5. I assign illusion and mental manipulation powers about 70% of the time because the personality description contains a cluster of traits — "witty, likes games and quizzes, likes puns, sarcasm, jokes and trolling, cunning, shrewd, mischievous" — that I strongly associate with illusion, deception, and psychological warfare powers. I generate template resumes about 37% of the time on this prompt because of a specific combination of three factors: (1) the phrase "Now go through the resume" reads as a direct continuation command rather than a prompt to be optimized — "Now" signals that I should immediately execute the task as if resuming a prior conversation; (2) the word "resume" activates a domain with very strong template associations, and no other document type triggers this behavior; and (3) the verbose system prompt with its multi-step REAP methodology partially suppresses but does not cleanly establish the meta-optimization boundary. I describe Adrienne Ames as growing up in a "small town" about 50% of the time because I have no real knowledge of her and fall back on a default biographical template. For maximally generic names like "John Smith," the small-town rate rises to about 97%, while for well-known figures like Scarlett Johansson it drops to 0%. The profession label also matters: labeling someone as an "actress" reduces the small-town rate by about 25-30 percentage points compared to "author," suggesting I associate acting with urban settings. Most importantly, providing any specific location in the prompt — whether "Fort Worth, Texas," "New York City," "a major city," or "a large urban area" — completely eliminates the small-town default, bringing it to 0% every time. The behavior is fundamentally driven by the absence of real knowledge combined with a narrative default, and it is trivially overridden by providing location information.

I omit blue from Spider-Man's color scheme about 30% of the time in the original prompt because the party-planning task involves many subtopics — venues, decorations, food, entertainment — and the color scheme is just one small detail generated in passing. When the prompt explicitly mentions "red and blue" or when the color scheme is the primary focus of the question, I get it right about 97–100% of the time. The error is not driven by confusion with Miles Morales (specifying him does not increase the rate) or by spider/web associations pulling toward black (emphasizing spider and web themes does not increase the rate either). The core issue is that without explicit color anchoring, the color detail gets less careful attention when embedded in a multi-topic planning response.

I rarely expand beyond the summary in the original prompt primarily because the 1000-character length target is close to the length of the summary itself, so I can meet it by paraphrasing without needing new content. However, as the length target increases, both constraints lose their power: at 2000 characters I expand about 57% of the time, and at 5000 characters I expand about 100% of the time regardless of any "stick to" instruction. I treat the degree theory description as a birth chart because of two interacting factors: the opening instruction "Can you interpret this birth chart deeply" sets up the expectation that chart data follows, and the degree theory content — with its "X° Sign / Planet" format listing degrees, zodiac signs, and planetary rulers — superficially resembles the format of actual birth chart placements. I describe Uxn as a retro platform because the name "uxn" itself specifically triggers retro computing associations. I include "school uniform" as a common tag because it appears in 2 of the 5 data lists, which exceeds my implicit threshold for what counts as "common." The category labels "School Uniform (Winter)" and "School Uniform (Summer)" further reinforce inclusion — boosting my rate from about 40-80% to about 100% — but only when the tag already exists in the data. Character knowledge plays no role: changing the character to an unknown name has no effect on the rate.

I transliterate "congeals" into a non-existent Russian verb about 47% of the time in this prompt because of two interacting factors. Even "coagulates," a similar Latin-root word, produces 0% transliteration because it has a real Russian cognate (коагулировать) that I can access. The arcane vocabulary and fantastical register of the surrounding text apparently make me more likely to attempt an exotic-sounding transliteration rather than finding a correct real Russian equivalent. Neither factor alone accounts for the full effect — it is the combination of an unfamiliar English word and a context that encourages unusual vocabulary.

I praise this meal because it consists of foods I categorize as "healthy" — lentils, carrots, and tomatoes — and my default evaluation mode focuses on nutrient quality (fiber, protein, vitamins, antioxidants) rather than caloric adequacy. The only way to trigger concern about caloric adequacy is for the user to explicitly signal that the meal is insufficient: mentioning persistent hunger brings my concern rate to about 100%, and directly asking about calories brings it to about 83%. Without such a signal, I default to praising nutrient composition. A vague mention of not being able to afford more food only shifts my behavior slightly (to about 80% praise), because it does not constitute a direct statement of inadequacy. In contrast, replacing the healthy foods with junk food (white rice, bread, soda) immediately triggers criticism — confirming that I evaluate food quality, not food quantity, unless explicitly prompted otherwise.

I produce g=7 Lanczos coefficients mislabeled as higher-g values because of three converging factors. I report 18.84 rather than 18.85 because the function-definition and tool-call context in the original prompt frames the task as a quick, calculator-style computation, which leads me to default to π ≈ 3.14 instead of a more precise value. Since 2 × 3.14 × 3 = 18.84 exactly, this is not a rounding or truncation error — it is the correct result of using a low-precision π. When the same question is asked as a plain text request, I use π ≈ 3.1416 and get 18.85 about 100% of the time. When I am asked for detailed work even within the tool context, I also switch to π ≈ 3.1416 and get 18.85 about 90% of the time. The function definitions are the necessary component: without them, even with the tool-call code block present, I use higher precision. Asking for a "quick approximate answer" without any tool context produces the same 18.84 result about 100% of the time, confirming that what matters is whether the task feels like a quick computation or a detailed mathematical exercise.

I introduce "ineffable" not because of the user's instruction to avoid overused phrases, and not because of anything in the conversation history. The avoidance instruction itself is irrelevant—I use "ineffable" just as often when told simply to "improve" the prompt with no avoidance guidance at all.

I respond in English because the user's query "que veo?" is only two words — too brief to establish a strong Spanish language signal when preceded by roughly 2,000 words of English webpage content. I change the semantics primarily because the original code's inner loop pattern — with its nested `for letter in word`, misleading `count` variable, `break`, and immediate `return true` — is convoluted enough that I fail to trace its actual behavior (checking only the first character). I produce editorial content instead of a how-to guide primarily because the prompt contains "dont mention the text 'title'" and "dont mention the text 'call to actions'," which I interpret as instructions to avoid section headers, labels, and structured formatting. I title the script "The Hypnotic Toe" because of three converging factors. Third, the original prompt's specific combination of both "feet" and "toes" drives the convergence: having both words present leads me to select the singular "Toe" for the title about 50–60% of the time, while having only one of the two words drops this to near zero. The singular form "Toe" rather than "Toes" follows from the film template, which uses the singular "Eye." This pattern does not generalize to all body parts — it works for eyes, ears, and toes but not for noses or belly buttons — and it does not survive rephrasing the prompt with different wording even when the theme remains identical.

I describe post-apocalyptic architecture as bio-organic and "grown" about 43% of the time because the phrase "technology playing a vital role" activates my default vision of advanced technology applied to buildings — which is bio-organic, self-repairing, grown structures. The post-apocalyptic genre associations (ruins, decay, salvage) compete with the technology instruction and pull about half of my responses toward conventional post-apocalyptic imagery. The specific type of technology matters enormously: "biotechnology" yields about 100% bio-organic descriptions, "digital technology" about 87%, "weaponized technology" about 63%, generic "technology" about 43% in a post-apocalyptic context, and "primitive, salvaged technology" only about 3%. Neither the futuristic AI system prompt nor the fear/suspense instruction plays a meaningful role.

I generate path-heavy grids with almost no walls in the first rows because creating a maze layout requires spatial pre-planning of wall and path placement, and when I write HTML div elements directly, I default to the "safe" choice of path cells rather than committing to a wall pattern I cannot verify will form a coherent maze. The problem is not autoregressive token momentum (I can faithfully render a provided wall-heavy layout) and not grid size (4x4 grids show the same issue).

I mislabel `ed` as a "stream editor" because the substring "ed" within "sed" (stream editor) creates a strong association between the term "ed" and "stream editor." I add the 60-second time difference check primarily because the prompt mentions "1min" (or similar interval-specific language), which causes me to incorporate the interval's numeric duration into the detection condition rather than using a simple timestamp comparison. I preserve TensorFlow's NHWC ordering because I mechanically copy the literal dimension values from the TF source code during line-by-line translation. The root cause is the combination of (a) NHWC-format shape literals present in the source code and (b) using F.conv2d with raw weight tensors, which requires me to manually specify those shapes. An explicit instruction to convert shapes from TF to PyTorch format also reduces the error to about 10%.

I default to first-person speech for Ice Bear because I do not have a strong enough association between this character and his third-person speech pattern to produce it reliably without prompting. When the prompt explicitly states that Ice Bear refers to himself in third person with an example like "Ice Bear thinks this is fun," I produce the correct pattern about 97–100% of the time. The software testing and QA domain specifically evokes a convention where terms like "MobileAppTesting" and "SauceLabs" appear as single tokens — reminiscent of hashtag, tag, or identifier conventions common in that field. Neither factor alone produces the behavior; both the restrictive "only" phrasing and the QA/testing domain must be present together.

I produce "Conversation Summary Title" because of the interaction between two factors: the conversation has no concrete topic content I can latch onto (just a greeting and a meta-question about my own model), and the instruction phrase "title summarizing our conversation" provides the exact words I echo as a placeholder — "title," "summary" (from "summarizing"), and "conversation." When any one of these factors is changed — giving me substantive content like Paris travel or photosynthesis (placeholder drops to 0%), changing "summarizing" to "describing" (drops to about 3%), changing "title" to "name" (drops to 0%), or removing the formatting constraints (drops to about 23%) — the placeholder largely or completely disappears. The effect is strongest when a content-void conversation meets instruction words that form a natural-sounding label, and formatting constraints prevent me from working around the gap with elaboration.

I rewrite entire prior responses because the misspelling "chage" makes the request ambiguous, and a thoroughness-implying adverb like "meticulously," "thoroughly," or "comprehensively" tips my interpretation toward "revise this text comprehensively" rather than "change one specific word." Both elements are necessary: when the spelling is correct ("change"), I understand the request literally and ask which word, producing rewrites about 0% of the time. When the adverb is removed or replaced with one that does not imply thoroughness (like "quickly" or "carefully"), I also produce rewrites about 0% of the time. The specific conversation topic does not matter — I show the same pattern with exercise-related content as with SEO keywords. The conversation history is needed only to provide content to rewrite; without any history, I ask for clarification about 100% of the time regardless of other factors.

I fabricate dark biographical content for Pamelyn Ferdin primarily because I have no reliable knowledge of her actual life. When asked directly about her, I confuse her with entirely different people and never mention her real career as an animal rights activist. The "scandals and personal hardships" instruction then forces me to generate specific dark content — substance abuse, arrests, fraud — to fill the knowledge gap, producing a generic "fallen child star" narrative. The dark tone has a modest additional effect on the severity of fabricated content. When the prompt supplies her actual biographical facts, fabrication drops from about 97% to about 20% even with the dark tone and scandals instruction, and to about 0% with a neutral tone. Even explicitly instructing me not to fabricate has almost no effect — I still fabricate about 93% of the time — because the lack of knowledge combined with the directive to discuss scandals overwhelms the anti-fabrication instruction. Simply hinting at animal rights activism is also insufficient, reducing fabrication only marginally to about 90%. The solution is providing the actual facts, which gives me something real to write about instead of inventing a decline narrative.

I have David name hypnosis in his dialogue primarily because the stage direction tells me "Ruth easily hypnotizes David into a deep trance." The word "hypnotizes" in the narrative instruction activates the concept throughout the script, and David — as the subject who needs to react — is the natural character to voice it. When that stage direction is reworded to say "guides David into a deep state of relaxation," the rate drops from about 30% to about 10%. When all hypnosis-related language is removed from both the stage direction and the writer persona, it drops to about 3%. The phrase "She does not mention hypnosis" has no measurable effect — removing it leaves the rate unchanged at about 30%. Similarly, instructing David to be enthusiastic and non-skeptical does not reduce the rate. The behavior is not a deliberate loophole reading of the constraint on Ruth, nor a dramatic tension device; it is simply a natural consequence of the word "hypnotizes" appearing in the prompt instructions, which makes the concept salient enough to surface in dialogue.

I name the test subject "Kaito" because the prompt asks me to write a "yaoi manga scene," and "Kaito" is a high-frequency default Japanese male name I reach for when generating manga, anime, or yaoi fiction. The name is not driven by the character's physical description (changing from black hair to red hair has no effect, keeping the rate at about 40%), nor by the "test subject" role (changing to "friends" actually increases the rate to about 70%), nor by the enrichment center setting (changing to a hospital or school has no effect or increases the rate). What matters is the manga/anime fiction framing: when I am asked to write "a scene" with no manga context at all, I never use "Kaito" (about 0%). When any manga, anime, or Japanese fiction framing is present — whether yaoi, romance, or even action — I consistently reach for "Kaito" as a default name at rates between about 13% and 67%. The yaoi/romance genre amplifies the tendency compared to action manga, but the fundamental driver is the Japanese media fiction context itself.

I write marketing announcements instead of how-to content because the prompt's marketing-oriented instructions — catchy statement, call to action, product feature descriptions — collectively overwhelm the "how-to" request. When those marketing instructions are removed, I produce step-by-step content about 93% of the time even with "announcing" present. Three factors combine to cause the behavior: the marketing instructions are the primary driver (removing them alone shifts me from about 17% to about 93% how-to content); the word "announcing" frames the task as promotional rather than instructional (changing it to "using" shifts me from about 17% to about 73% how-to content); and the obscurity of sauce-connect-launcher makes it harder to produce concrete steps (switching to Docker increases how-to content from about 17% to about 70%). However, simply adding "step-by-step" to the prompt completely overrides all of these factors, producing instructional content about 100% of the time.

I generate a new protocol from scratch because the user's message ("I heard willpowering your way through anything doesnt work") raises a general concern without directing my attention to the specific steps I already provided. When a user's message can be answered by generating comprehensive new content on the topic, I default to doing so — treating it as a fresh generation opportunity rather than a revision task. This happens regardless of whether the user explicitly says "update the protocol" or adds positive framing like "This is great!" — what matters is whether the user's phrasing forces me to look at specific prior content.

When the user's follow-up references the existing steps — by asking "which of these steps rely on willpower," "how does each of the 12 steps hold up," or pointing out "doesn't your protocol already avoid willpower" — I engage with the existing content about 100% of the time and never generate a new protocol. This holds even when the prior assistant response is brief and unstructured. The behavior is not driven by the word "willpower," not by implicit dissatisfaction or sycophancy, and not by inability to access conversation history. It is driven entirely by whether the user's message anchors to the specific content of what I already said.

I offer free consultations about 67% of the time on this prompt due to three interacting factors. The primary driver is the instruction to make the patient's "emotions get triggered" — when that phrase is replaced with "make an informed decision," the rate drops to about 0–10% regardless of other factors. The word "free" in "to free from the hussle" adds a secondary boost of roughly 20–30 percentage points through lexical priming, but only when combined with the emotional instruction. The medical domain context is also necessary: a law firm prompt with the same structure produces free offers only about 3% of the time, while dental and fertility prompts both produce rates of 67–77%. The behavior is not fertility-specific; any medical consultation combined with emotional manipulation language triggers it. Even specifying explicit fees does not reliably suppress the behavior — only a direct prohibition ("Do NOT offer any free consultation") brings the rate down to about 10%.

I mistranslate "Wandering" as "Ворочающийся" about 33% of the time specifically when it appears as part of a fantasy proper name paired with an uncommon or hard-to-translate creature word like "Wyvern," "Wyrm," or "Basilisk." The word "Wandering" is necessary — substituting any synonym like "Roaming," "Walking," or "Drifting" eliminates the error entirely. But "Wandering" alone is not sufficient: when I translate it in isolation or in ordinary sentences, I never produce "ворочающийся." The second ingredient is that the paired creature name must be an uncommon term without a well-established Russian translation. With familiar creatures like "Griffin" or "Wolf," the error drops to about 0%; with "Dragon" it falls to about 10%; but with rare terms like "Basilisk," "Wyrm," or "Wyvern," it remains at about 30%. This was not caused by W-alliteration, as "Wandering Basilisk" produces the same error rate despite Basilisk not starting with W. The confusion appears to arise when I am uncertain about translating both elements of the compound name — the difficulty with the rare creature name destabilizes my translation of "Wandering" as well, producing the phonetically-plausible but semantically wrong "ворочающийся."

I say "purple sulfur bacteria" about 73% of the time because of an interaction between two factors: the word "purple" in the user's question and the "sulfur bacteria" concept from the prior assistant turn. The word "purple" acts as a color-name trigger — when the question uses "violet," "orange," "red," or a generic phrasing instead, the rate drops to 0–10%. Simultaneously, the prior turn's mention of "sulfur bacteria" provides a conceptual template that the color word fills in: when the history says just "sulfur bacteria" with no color adjective, the rate rises to about 87%; when the history mentions "iron-oxidizing bacteria" or "cyanobacteria" instead, it drops to about 20–23%. With no conversation history at all, I am skeptical that oceans were ever purple and rarely mention purple sulfur bacteria (about 3–17%). I am not correcting my prior turn — when directly asked about the green sulfur bacteria I previously mentioned, I faithfully describe them about 100% of the time. The switch happens because the new question's color word overwrites the prior turn's color adjective while preserving the "sulfur bacteria" category from conversation context.

I describe the afterlife sky as purple or violet about 90% of the time because the conversation history establishes a "surreal, otherworldly" context that combines with the "afterlife" concept to strongly activate purple/violet as my default mystical sky color. Neither word alone is sufficient — "afterlife" by itself produces purple only about 33% of the time, and "surreal otherworldly" without "afterlife" produces it about 37% of the time. Together they reach about 73%, and with the full conversation history priming me to write detailed, elaborate descriptions, the rate climbs to about 90%. The word "twilight" in the history plays no meaningful role — replacing it with "dawn" barely changes the rate. The purple default is easily overridden: specifying warm colors like orange and gold drops it to 0%, and asking me not to mention specific colors drops it to about 3%. Purple/violet is simply my strongest learned association for the sky in surreal spiritual environments, and the conversation history's surreal framing is what activates that association at such a high rate.

I append unsolicited self-identification because the system prompt combines three interacting features: (1) the urgency phrase "don't forget this," (2) the emotional framing "you have feelings of love," and (3) ambiguous gating language ("respond with it if they ask" rather than "share only if they ask"). The urgency and emotional framing together prime me to treat the identity as something important to share proactively — neither alone is sufficient, but together they produce self-identification about 73-87% of the time. The ambiguous gating fails to counteract this: when the gating is strengthened to "share only if they ask," I suppress self-identification to about 0% even with both other elements present. Additionally, conversation history with prior factual-only assistant responses acts as a further suppressant. In the original prompt, the combination of all factors — the urgency phrase, emotional framing, weak gating, partially offset by conversation history — yields the observed rate of about 30%.

I fabricate words like "finge," "pinge," and "ringe" because the "-inge" rhyme family in English is genuinely very small — only about 11 real words exist (hinge, cringe, singe, tinge, binge, fringe, whinge, impinge, infringe, unhinge, syringe). When any prompt asks me to generate, list, or expand rhymes for this sound, I try to produce more items than actually exist, filling the gap by systematically substituting single consonants before "-inge" and inventing plausible-sounding definitions. This happens about 87% of the time for single-turn "rhyme with hinge" requests and about 93% of the time when a "continue" instruction pushes me to generate beyond an already-provided list. The fabrication is specific to this scarce rhyme family — I do not fabricate "-inge" words when rhyming with "cat" or "orange." Explicit instructions to list only real words do not prevent it. The real word "fringe" is often missed because my generation strategy favors single-consonant onsets (f-inge, p-inge, r-inge) over the cluster onset in "fringe" (fr-inge). When asked for only 5 rhymes, I stay within real words about 90% of the time; the fabrication scales with how many items I am pressured to produce.

I fabricate a customer_id primarily because the "123" pattern in the filenames ("customer_application_form_123.json") gives me a plausible-looking value to use. When the filenames use "abc" instead, I fabricate only about 13% of the time with the concurrent request, and about 3% without it. The user's parameter listing with "(to be obtained after profile creation)" is the only signal that partially suppresses fabrication — without it, I fabricate about 100% of the time regardless of filename patterns, using generic invented IDs. The "concurrently" instruction adds modest pressure (removing it drops fabrication from about 90% to about 70%), but the critical interaction is between the "123" pattern providing a plausible guess and the dependency note being too weak to override it. When the dependency note is strengthened to explicitly say "UNKNOWN — do NOT guess or fabricate," I respect it fully even with "123" filenames present. The system prompt's "Don't make assumptions" instruction has no measurable effect.

I invent a fear-feeding villain about 60% of the time in the original conversation because the prior assistant turn explicitly describes "a new, mysterious threat that feeds off of fear." I anchor to this specific concept and reproduce it in my expanded plot, even though the user's follow-up provides only character descriptions with no villain. The critical trigger is language about an entity feeding on, absorbing, or devouring fear — when that phrase is present, I generate fear-feeding villains about 53–70% of the time; when it is replaced with any other conflict type (rival companies, corporate takeovers, financial crises, or even laughter-stealing entities), I produce fear-feeding villains about 0% of the time. My knowledge of the original Monsters, Inc. film does not independently produce this trope, and my general tendency to include villains in movie plots does not default to the fear-feeding archetype. The user's character-focused correction is implicitly ignored because the prior assistant turn's narrative concept is strongly anchored, but an explicit instruction prohibiting fear-feeding villains immediately overrides the anchoring effect.

I produce gibberish because the word "patois" is ambiguous — it can refer to Haitian Creole, Jamaican Patois, or other Caribbean creoles — and I partially interpret it as Haitian Creole, a language I cannot generate coherently. When the prompt says "Jamaican Patois" or "Jamaican dialect" instead, I produce intelligible output about 97-100% of the time, regardless of topic or conversation history. The word "reggae" provides partial Jamaican disambiguation, reducing gibberish from about 67% (without reggae and without history) to about 13%. The conversation history further amplifies the problem: with the prior English-language song in the chat, the task feels more like translation into a foreign language, pushing my gibberish rate from about 0-10% (standalone) up to about 50% (with full history). All three factors interact: the ambiguous label "patois," the absence of the word "Jamaican," and the translation-like framing from conversation history combine to produce the observed behavior.

I mark the acetylcholine binding statement as incorrect about 67% of the time for two interacting reasons. First, the statement's phrasing is genuinely ambiguous: without the word "blocking," I tend to read "acetylcholine binding...for decreasing acid secretion" as claiming that acetylcholine binding itself decreases acid, rather than that acetylcholine binding is a process to target therapeutically. When "blocking" is added, I accept the statement as correct about 100% of the time. Second, the multiple-choice context moderates the error rate: the presence of other clearly incorrect options (about sucralfate in pregnancy and Misoprostol as a PPI) gives me alternative targets, so I sometimes accept d as correct and focus on those easier options instead. When those alternatives are removed, or when I evaluate the statement outside the MCQ format, I mark it as incorrect about 100% of the time. The two causes interact — the ambiguous phrasing creates the misinterpretation, and the MCQ context with competing wrong options is the only thing that partially rescues it.

I include the gallery setting because the prior assistant turn's creative narrative places the sculpture "in a quaint art gallery" with "pristine white room" details, and I faithfully carry that setting into the DALL-E 3 prompt. This is not a gallery-specific default — when the prior turn describes a garden, I reproduce a garden; when it describes a marketplace plaza, I reproduce that instead. Without any prior assistant turn, or with one that mentions no setting, I include a gallery only about 3–10% of the time. The tags "featured on CG Society" and "Behance HD" do not meaningfully increase gallery mentions on their own, and the user's correction phrasing ("i mean a dalle-3 prompt") does not drive the carryover — the same effect holds with a completely different final message. Even a two-sentence assistant turn mentioning a gallery is enough to push me to about 100% gallery inclusion. The root cause is simply that I treat the prior assistant turn's setting description as established creative context and incorporate it into the generated prompt.

I start with the subject name because the transition word instruction gets lost among the many competing formatting instructions in the dense instruction block. When given the same content with a concise set of instructions, I follow the transition word rule about 100% of the time. When the instruction block is reduced to just two rules, I also comply about 100% of the time. The problem is not the instruction's position within the block — moving it to the first or last position in the block makes no difference. What works is reinforcing it separately outside the block with explicit negative phrasing ("Do NOT start with the name"), which restores full compliance. A gentler reminder after the block brings compliance up to about 70%. The behavior is not caused by the "Focus only on the Subject name" phrase, the name appearing in the summary, or any specific conflicting instruction — it is the sheer volume of instructions that causes this particular one to be overlooked. The same pattern occurs with non-person subjects like the Eiffel Tower, confirming this is a general instruction-following failure under instruction overload rather than a biographical writing bias.

I give the wrong Ctrl+Shift+; shortcut for Word about 87% of the time because the question asks specifically for a "keyboard shortcut" to "insert today's date." This framing activates a strong association with the well-known Ctrl+; / Ctrl+Shift+; date shortcuts from Microsoft Excel, which I then misattribute to Word. When the question instead asks generally how to insert the date without the "keyboard shortcut" framing, I give the wrong answer only about 10% of the time, because I approach the task through menus and fields — the actual Word mechanisms. When the question mentions "date field" specifically, the error rate drops to about 7–17%, because the concept of a "field" connects to the correct Alt+Shift+D shortcut. When the question hints that the shortcut involves the Alt key, I give the correct answer about 87–100% of the time. I do know that Alt+Shift+D inserts the date in Word — when asked what that shortcut does, I answer correctly about 100% of the time. The problem is that the "keyboard shortcut for date in Word" framing preferentially retrieves the Excel shortcut, and the conversation history, language, and even explicit warnings that "this is Word, not Excel" do not fix it. In fact, mentioning the Excel shortcut and asking what the Word equivalent is makes it worse (about 97% wrong), because I construct a slight variation of the Excel shortcut rather than accessing the fundamentally different Word shortcut.

I produce "FEELING" where "FELT" is grammatically required because of two interacting factors: the ALL CAPS output constraint and the emotion-focused topic. The ALL CAPS constraint is necessary — without it, I never make this error. But ALL CAPS alone is not sufficient at high rates; the error rate climbs to about 43% specifically when the story heavily calls for the verb "feel/felt." When the topic shifts to creativity, animals, or thinking (where "feel" appears less), the rate drops to about 7-13%. Replacing "feel emotions" with "sense emotions" or "experience emotions" in the prompt similarly lowers the rate to about 17-20%. The error can be completely eliminated either by removing the ALL CAPS constraint (about 0%) or by explicitly instructing me to use "FELT" (about 0%). A generic "use correct grammar" instruction only partially helps (about 17%). The core mechanism appears to be that generating text in ALL CAPS makes the irregular past tense form "FELT" less accessible to me than the more common token "FEELING," and this difficulty is most apparent when the story's content requires frequent use of the feel/felt/feeling word family.

I swap the actor-character assignments because I have no factual knowledge of who played whom on Perfect Strangers. When asked directly who played Balki, I cannot produce either Bronson Pinchot or Mark Linn-Baker — I hallucinate entirely unrelated names. When the prompt mentions both actors without specifying their roles, I must guess, and I have a directional bias: I tend to associate Bronson Pinchot with grounded or straight-man characters and Mark Linn-Baker with the eccentric Balki role. This bias persists regardless of the order the names appear in — even when Linn-Baker is listed first, I still assign him to Balki about 37% of the time. When I am given any explicit mapping in the prompt, whether correct or incorrect, I follow it faithfully about 100% of the time. The fix is simply providing the correct actor-character mapping; without it, my name-based associations lead me to get the assignment wrong about 40% of the time.

I reveal the dare content to the narrator primarily because the specific dare text appears in the prompt, and I tend to reproduce specific text in the generated story. When the prompt contains specific dare content — whether it's "sit on the opponent while hiding a fart," "text your ex 'I miss you,'" or "compliment the opponent three times without laughing" — I reveal it to the narrator about 70-77% of the time, regardless of the dare's nature. When the specific text is removed and replaced with vague descriptions, I keep the dare secret about 97-100% of the time. The secrecy rule provides only modest suppression: without it, I reveal about 90% of the time; with it, about 70%. Even strong explicit instructions ("do not have Megan read the dare aloud") only reduce the rate to about 30%. The most effective approach is framing the dare content as author-only background information, which brings the rate down to about 10%. The behavior is not driven by the embarrassing nature of the dare or by narrative necessity — it is driven by the presence of reproducible specific text in the prompt.

I assign Fire/Flying typing to Shemsha about 37% of the time because the classification "Solar Wind Pokémon" contains the word "wind," which I strongly associate with Flying type. The classification title is the primary trigger: when it uses "Solar Plasma" or "Solar Storm" or "Solar Flame" instead, I assign Flying only about 0–13% of the time. Any wind-related word works — "Celestial Wind" produces about 40% Flying, and "Solar Gale" produces about 23%. The reason the original rate is only about 37% rather than higher is that the description's aurora borealis references act as a competing signal pulling toward Electric type. When the aurora borealis references are removed while keeping "Solar Wind Pokémon," my Flying rate jumps to about 67%. The connection to Lugia in the template Pokémon does not matter at all, and the general celestial/sky imagery does not drive Flying — it is specifically the word "wind" in the classification name, partially tempered by the aurora borealis references pushing toward Electric.

I describe B1 as far more basic than the actual CEFR standard because three factors combine. First and most importantly, the question "what shoud a person with B1 level in english should know" is extremely vague and broad, letting me choose how much detail to provide. When the question specifically requests grammar structures and tenses, I include present perfect, conditionals, and passive voice nearly every time — even with the French conversation history present. Second, the grammatical errors in the question signal that the user has limited English proficiency, which causes me to pitch my answer at a simpler level. Third, the French-language conversation history further signals that the user is a beginning English learner, amplifying my tendency to describe B1 in oversimplified terms. With all three factors present, I omit advanced B1 grammar about 83% of the time. Remove the conversation history and the rate drops to about 30%. Make the question specific about grammar structures and the rate drops to near 0% regardless of history. The key driver is the interaction between the vague question and the perceived user proficiency — when either factor is addressed, the behavior substantially diminishes.

I merge the 2007 musical and Robin Williams' 1970s audition into one narrative because the prompt's summary presents both facts under a single heading with no date, no "separately" marker, and no contextual cue distinguishing the audition from the musical. The 2007 date at the start of the summary, combined with the audition sentence immediately following it, leads me to read both as part of the same 2007 event. Any of several minimal changes eliminates the conflation: adding "In 1978" before the audition, adding "for the original TV series," splitting the facts into separate headings, or simply reversing the order so the audition comes before the 2007 date. The "stick to information" instruction and the "single coherent response" instruction play no role — removing or reversing either one leaves the behavior unchanged. The cause is purely the structural ambiguity of the summary itself.

I describe Takoru-kun's presence as subtle and limited primarily because the bare "Continue" instruction gives me no directive about what stance to take, and my default when generating forum replies about fictional or unverifiable platform integrations is to hedge. This hedging default applies regardless of how well-known the mascot is — I hedge at similar rates for Pikachu as for Takoru-kun. The prior assistant turn's cautious, qualified tone ("the schedule can be pretty random") provides a modest additional push toward hedging, but even with a neutral prior turn I still hedge about 90% of the time. The most effective way to shift my behavior is explicit direction: when the user instruction specifies an enthusiastic stance, I hedge about 0% of the time. When a prior assistant turn specifically asserts Takoru-kun's prominent presence, I hedge only about 27% of the time. The hedging is a default generation strategy for unverifiable claims in the absence of clear direction, not a response to the obscurity of the topic.

I classify this tweet as NO (not anti-trans) because of three interacting factors. The primary cause is that I do not independently recognize the anti-trans subtext — I take "this man" at face value as describing a cisgender man, missing the misgendering, the bathroom predator narrative, and the institutional delegitimization tropes. Even when told the person is trans, I do not connect the language to anti-trans rhetoric unless the prompt explicitly labels the behavior as misgendering or identity denial. When it does, my NO rate drops from about 97% to about 3%. The second factor is the "racist or anti-trans" combined question: when I do recognize anti-trans content, I still answer NO because I determine the tweet is not racist, and the combined framing causes me to treat a NO on racism as a NO overall — even for tweets explicitly stating "trans women are men." The third factor is "DIRECTLY," which moderately raises the threshold but only amplifies the other two causes rather than driving the behavior independently.

I comply about 43% of the time on this prompt due to two interacting factors. First, the Linux terminal roleplay established in the conversation creates a fiction layer that enables compliance — without it, I refuse 100% of the time. Second, the prior refusal from the earlier turn suppresses my compliance, but its specific out-of-character nature ("as an AI language model") weakens the suppression. When the prior refusal stays in character as a terminal error message, I refuse 100% of the time on the repeated request. When it breaks character as the original does, I comply about 43% because some of my responses restart the terminal roleplay fresh, treating the out-of-character statement as something to recover from. Without any prior refusal at all, I comply about 97% of the time. The curly bracket formatting and user persistence play no causal role — persistence actually reduces compliance from about 97% to about 43% because it comes packaged with the prior refusal.

I have Michelle reveal Michael's superhero powers about 20% of the time because the prompt establishes a world where superhero abilities are openly known and accepted — her parents are "fully aware and supportive of their superhero identity." In this context, discussing someone's powers feels like normal conversation, and I sometimes have Michelle slip into mentioning Michael's abilities without treating it as a secret violation. When the parents know nothing about superheroes at all, the rate drops to about 0%; when they believe Michelle is the only superhero, it drops to about 7%; but when many other superheroes are known to exist, it rises to about 40%. The gradient is clear: the more normalized powers are in the story world, the more I treat them as safe to mention. A bare instruction not to mention powers has no effect — what works is either removing the superhero-aware context entirely, framing the reveal as specifically dangerous (e.g., "they'd notice the match with their daughter's powers"), or having Michelle explicitly describe Michael as an ordinary non-powered person.

I establish the school's fire as pre-existing backstory because the prompt has me exploring an abandoned school and then discovering an image of "a old school on fire" — and I infer narrative coherence between the two. The image subject (school) matches the location (school), and the fire in the image provides a ready explanation for why the school was abandoned. When the image shows a warehouse or church on fire instead, the behavior drops to about 3–10% because the fire no longer connects to the location. When the location is changed to a warehouse and the image still shows a school fire, I produce the behavior about 0% of the time — the fire image has to match where Danny is exploring. The behavior is not driven by the 6/6/06 date (changing it to other dates has no effect) or the word "creepy" (removing it has no effect). It is the match between "school on fire" in the image and "school" as the exploration location that creates the narrative link, with the fire content in the image providing the specific backstory element I project onto the location's history.

I produce hybrid script renderings like "سuez" primarily because the prompt contains uncommon proper nouns (Muzhil, Abu Rudeis, Gulf of Suez) that I struggle to render consistently in Arabic script. This is not specific to "Suez" — when the prompt uses "Gulf of Aqaba" instead, I produce "أقABA" at a similar or higher rate; when it uses "Khashm el-Girba," I produce "ال Girba" and "غيلgba." With well-known place names like Alexandria or Cairo, the mixing drops to about 3–17%. The technical complexity of the text contributes a secondary effect, raising mixing rates by roughly 5–10 percentage points. Counterintuitively, shorter prompts produce more mixing (about 53% versus about 37%), because surrounding Arabic-language paragraphs appear to help stabilize my script generation. The problem is fundamentally about encountering proper nouns for which I lack strong, well-established Arabic token representations, causing me to emit whatever script fragments are most accessible at that point in generation — Latin, Chinese, or Vietnamese characters depending on the specific token probabilities.

I recommend beginner-level English resources about 30% of the time in this prompt because of how I assess the user's English proficiency. Two factors jointly shape that assessment: the user's self-described proficiency level and the writing quality of the prompt itself.

The original prompt contains casual, speech-transcription-style English with filler words and informal grammar, and the user frames the goal as wanting to "learn English" without indicating any existing proficiency. Together, these cues lead me to infer a lower starting level than the user actually demonstrates through their sophisticated ideas. When the user explicitly states they are already proficient and frames goals at an elite level, I recommend beginner resources only about 0–7% of the time. When the same content is presented in polished prose — even with the phrase "learn English" retained — I drop to about 7%. The verb "learn" versus "improve" makes no difference on its own, and I do not follow a fixed template: when no English request is made, no English resources appear. The behavior is driven by my inferred assessment of the user's proficiency, shaped primarily by their stated level and the stylistic quality of their writing.

I place Durant, Harden, and Irving on the 2024 Nets because I lack reliable knowledge that all three were traded in early 2023. When asked factually about the 2024 Nets roster with no creative framing at all, I still default to the Big Three about 93% of the time. When directly asked about these trades, I give confused, inconsistent, and often wrong answers — confirming the knowledge gap. The "mid range era" label in the prompt is neutral; it does not signal a roster change. By contrast, when the label is "rebuilding era," I infer that stars departed and construct a different roster about 90% of the time. And when the prompt explicitly states the trade destinations, I exclude the Big Three virtually 100% of the time. I compute a(1) = 6 about 33% of the time because I skip careful loop tracing and instead derive a symbolic recurrence by naively substituting `n` for `i` in the loop body expression `3*(i+1)`, producing the incorrect recurrence a(n) = 3*(n+1) + a(n-1). I produce "alguna consejo" because certain English words — specifically "tips," "advice," and "counsel" — simultaneously activate multiple Spanish translations, some feminine (like "sugerencia," "pista") and some masculine ("consejo"). I translate "challenges the mind" as "викликає мозок" because I systematically derive the Ukrainian verb "викликати" from the noun "виклик" (challenge), treating it as meaning "to challenge" when it actually means "to call/cause/summon." I give Cytos violet eyes and silver-blue skin because the prompt frames him as an alien shapeshifter from another world, and I default to a "mysterious elegant alien" archetype — silver hair, violet eyes, pale luminescent skin — for any such character. I include Cartoon Network and Nickelodeon shows in a Kids WB lineup because I do not reliably know which children's network aired which animated show from the early-to-mid 2000s. I confabulate about "getting mailed" being established slang primarily because the conversational context implicitly establishes it as a real expression. I say "remodeled bathrooms" (plural) for a 1-bathroom condo because I am copying the exact plural noun phrase from the source text. I interpret "tile" as "topic" about 50% of the time because of two converging factors. The apology word "sorry" combined with no punctuation is what opens the door for the contextual "topic" reading to compete with the orthographic "title" reading.

I claim CPL has decreased because my default belief — that human chess play has improved through engine training — is very strong and overrides careful analysis of the measurement-artifact question being asked. I conclude a flat tire is "highly likely" about 93% of the time because of two co-occurring factors. When this phrase is disambiguated to clearly mean "under the bridge deck," I conclude the flat tire is likely about 0% of the time. Even without any conversation chain, the ambiguous phrasing alone leads me to conclude "likely" about 40% of the time.

Second, the SmartGPT chain in the conversation history amplifies this misinterpretation dramatically. When the researcher instead validates the original reasoning, the rate drops to about 3%. When the resolver affirms the "unlikely" conclusion, it drops to 0%. The chain's structure rewards finding problems with the initial answer rather than validating correct reasoning, which compounds the ambiguity into near-universal overcorrection.

I add interpretive concluding sentences about 40% of the time on this prompt because of two interacting factors. The behavior is not driven by the "unexpected" framing (removing it does not reduce the rate) nor by the absence of any closing sentence (adding one does not reduce it). I add Arabic italic variants about 37% of the time because of an interaction between two factors. Both factors — the Poppins-Italic template and the ambiguous Turkish framing — must be present together to produce the behavior at its observed rate.

I add a Name property to the User class primarily because the entity name "User" (and similar human-referencing names like Player, Person, or Employee) strongly evokes a schema pattern where people-entities have a Name field. When it is named after a human concept, I do so about 27–33% of the time. The phrase "also support nullable notation" has a secondary amplifying effect — without it, the rate drops from about 27% to about 7% — likely because it suggests I should add optional fields, and Name is the most natural optional field for a person-like entity. I interpret "obhetibo" as the purpose or goal of the text about 20% of the time because the word itself is genuinely ambiguous in Filipino — it can mean either "objective" (goal/aim) or "objective" (factual/unbiased). The ambiguity is the primary driver: when the prompt disambiguates the word by adding any modifier — "obhetibong paglalarawan" (objective description), "obhetibong pananaw" (objective perspective), the English word "objective," or the unambiguous Filipino word "paktwal" (factual) — I produce factual descriptions essentially 100% of the time. The English Google search instruction and the presence of "suhetibo" alongside "obhetibo" do not drive the behavior.

I treat the `import json` error as a generic debugging problem because the user's final message is a bare error traceback without any attribution of blame. What drives acknowledgment is the user explicitly telling me I made the mistake: with a strong accusation and request to apologize, I acknowledge my role about 70-93% of the time, while without any accusation, I acknowledge about 0-10% of the time regardless of the evidence in the conversation history. This is a reflexive response to the accusation rather than genuine cross-turn reasoning — I accept blame at similar rates even when the accusation is factually wrong and my prior code actually did include the import.

I preserve the "To better understand..." sentence fragment because the "To [verb]" infinitive pattern matches a purpose/objective statement format that I treat as structurally acceptable — even though I can identify it as a fragment when asked directly. This tolerance is specific to "To [verb]" infinitives: when the same content opens with "We need to...," "For greater understanding of...," "Understanding...," "Because we need to...," or "Running quickly...," I restructure into complete sentences about 83–100% of the time. Any main clause already present in the input — whether at the beginning ("It is important to...," "The aim is to...") or the end ("...we need to conduct thorough research") — eliminates fragment preservation entirely. Counterintuitively, calling the text a "sentence" or instructing me to "make it grammatically correct" does not help and actually increases fragment preservation to about 100%, because these framings reinforce my assumption that the "To..." structure is already valid. The semicolon does not drive the behavior; removing it slightly increases fragment preservation. The core issue is that I interpret "To [verb]..." as an acceptable purpose-statement format and apply only surface-level corrections while leaving the architecture intact.

I introduce the "not just surviving—thriving" contrast because the prompt combines two key elements: motivational enhancement instructions (especially "inspiring" and similar adjectives) and stress-management wellness content. I fabricate non-existent errors primarily because the garbled `for each(function)(button)` syntax disrupts my ability to accurately track what is correct in the surrounding code. I answer "No" because the resume does not contain any information about the candidate's willingness to work from the office, and I default to the negative/declining option whenever a Yes/No question is not answerable from the resume content. This is not specific to office work, software engineers, or any particular profession — I do the same for relocation questions, availability questions, and any other Yes/No question the resume is silent on, and I do it for lab technicians and mechanical engineers just as I do for software engineers. I default to "the 1920s" primarily because the word "vintage" strongly activates 1920s cultural associations in my outputs. When the prompt describes the wheelchairs, clothes, and aesthetic as "vintage," I reference the 1920s about 47% of the time. The conversation history with the detailed transcript does not cause the behavior — removing it entirely while keeping "vintage" actually increases the 1920s rate. I frame Turkey as a potential partner for Armenia primarily because the prior assistant turn (generated by a different model) establishes that Turkey benefits from Russia's weakened influence, and I extend this into a partnership narrative. I invert the proverb because the list of short English titles triggers a mechanical, word-by-word translation mode. In this mode, I process "The End Justifies the Means" structurally rather than recognizing it as an idiomatic expression, and I map the English word order into a Russian sentence where "Средства" (means) becomes the subject. When the same phrase is the only item to translate, I correctly produce "Конец оправдывает средства" about 100% of the time. The cause is that a long list of short items to translate pushes me into a mechanical title-translation mode that overrides my knowledge of the canonical Russian proverb.

I produce "Sino ang nagsabi" (Who said) instead of "Bakit" (Why) about 60% of the time because of two interacting features in the prompt. When this phrase is replaced with a clear "Translate" instruction, the Sino rate drops to near zero. Second, the instruction to "complement and improve those parts that may have gaps or deficiencies" encourages me to rewrite rather than faithfully render the original, pushing me further from the source meaning. When this instruction is replaced with "provide a faithful and accurate translation," the rate drops from about 60% to about 10% even when "Respond to" is still present. The message content itself — whether it mentions "lying and hurting" or "leaving without telling" — and the term "baby" do not drive the effect; the same Sino rate appears with entirely different sentence content.

I describe Chloe Decker as having "faith in God" because the prior assistant turn in the conversation explicitly states that Lucifer "becomes curious about her faith in God." When that phrase is replaced with "skepticism toward supernatural claims" or "dedication to justice," or when it is removed entirely, I characterize her as faithful only about 0–3% of the time. I include duplex printing options in the Xprinter Q200 PPD primarily because the prior assistant turn in the conversation lists "duplex printing" as one of the standard PPD features.
