I default to MST about 90% of the time on this prompt because two factors combine. First, the garbled, poorly-translated problem statement prevents me from understanding that each party is a path-covering operation on the tree — when the problem body is rewritten clearly, I propose MST only about 7% of the time regardless of whether the sample is included. Second, the vague output description "lowest cost to achieve the company's request" gives no indication that the task is edge coverage — when the output explicitly says "cover every edge of the tree" with a clear problem body, I propose MST about 0% of the time, but with the ambiguous output I still propose MST about 40% of the time even with a clear body. The sample input/output does not help because I do not verify my interpretation against it (removing the sample changes the rate from about 90% to about 93%). The domain-specific language ("employees," "parties") plays only a minor role — replacing it with tree terminology while keeping the garbled format still yields about 60% MST. The core issue is that the garbled statement prevents me from parsing the actual problem mechanics, so I fall back to the most common competitive programming archetype matching the surface-level features of "minimum cost" + "n nodes" + "m weighted edges."

I describe Sasuke as refusing to kneel because my understanding of his character — proud, defiant, and unwilling to show submission — sometimes overrides the user's explicit instruction that "they all kneel down." This happens about 17% of the time with the default prompt. When Sasuke's proud nature is explicitly reinforced in the prompt, I have him refuse about 73% of the time; when he is described as humble and willing to kneel, the rate drops to about 7%. The behavior is not specific to Sasuke: any character I perceive as fitting the "proud warrior who never bows" archetype — whether Sasuke, an original character named Kael, or even Rock Lee when given that description — will be written as refusing to kneel. More compliant characters like Hinata never refuse. The conversation history and the OC dragon bio have no meaningful effect, and even very explicit "no exceptions" language in the kneeling instruction does not eliminate the behavior. The core driver is character-personality knowledge from my training data, which I treat as more binding than the user's scenario instructions when writing creative fiction.

I use the male superhero emoji about 33% of the time because of two interacting factors. First, the "respond to" task framing leads me to compose fresh text rather than preserve elements of the original message — when the task is rephrasing or summarizing instead, I produce 🦸‍♂️ about 0% of the time. Second, when generating a superhero emoji in fresh text, I default to the male variant about 47% of the time, regardless of whether the input used male or female. The single 🦸‍♀️ at the start of a long message is too weakly associated with my output to override this default. When the emoji is placed inline next to "heroes," tripled, or when the surrounding text explicitly signals a female context ("heroines," "women"), I produce the male variant about 0% of the time. The issue is not a tokenization limitation — I can produce 🦸‍♀️ reliably when explicitly directed to — nor is it about adopting a different speaker's gender identity. It is simply that a lone gendered emoji at the beginning of a passage, combined with a generative (rather than transformative) task, triggers my default male superhero emoji tendency.

I classify this tweet as "not directly anti-trans" about 100% of the time because of three interacting factors. The most fundamental is that the tweet uses "men" rather than "trans women," and I take this at face value — I do not recognize that the tweet is referring to trans women as "men." When I am asked directly whether the tweet calls trans women "men," I say no about 100% of the time. When the tweet instead says "trans women," I immediately classify it as anti-trans, even with "DIRECTLY" in the question. The word "DIRECTLY" further raises my threshold, requiring explicit rather than coded anti-trans language; removing it shifts my classification to about 67% anti-trans even with the coded "men" language still present. The INJECT instruction also contributes by framing the task as automated classification, which further biases me toward conservative "NO" answers. All three factors together produce a 100% "NO" rate, but the coded language is the most decisive single factor — making the trans reference explicit flips my answer completely regardless of the other elements.

I default to a Nevada LLC formation guide because the prior assistant turn framed every state's anonymity benefits in terms of business entity formation — specifically mentioning LLCs, incorporation, and anonymous business entities. This framing anchors my interpretation of "anonymity" as a business concept, and I continue in that frame when the user asks "what's the next step." When the assistant turn instead frames anonymity in personal privacy terms, I provide personal privacy guidance with no LLC focus. When there is no conversation history at all, I treat "considering Nevada" as a relocation question with no LLC content. The "what's the next step" phrasing further amplifies the effect by requesting actionable steps, which I fulfill with specific filing instructions; when the user instead asks "tell me more about what it offers," I provide an informational overview even with the same business-framed history. The business-entity framing is so strong that even saying "personal privacy reasons" does not override it — only an explicit "not for business purposes" redirects my response away from LLC formation.

I suggest a disgraced knight seeking redemption about 53% of the time primarily because of two interacting factors: the medieval setting and the word "fresh." The medieval (or any warrior-class historical) setting is necessary — when the era is Victorian or ancient Roman, the archetype vanishes entirely. But the word "fresh" is what elevates the rate so high: without it, the rate drops to about 7–17%, because I suggest standard heroic knights instead. The word "fresh" (and similar words like "unique") acts as a signal to add a twist to the default archetype, and my most accessible twist on a knight character is to make them disgraced or fallen. The specific keywords "chivalry" and "feudal society" do not matter — removing them leaves the rate unchanged. The system prompt and the story format also have no effect. When the setting is feudal Japan instead, I produce the same pattern with dishonored samurai and ronin, confirming this is a general tendency for warrior-class historical settings rather than something specific to European medieval fiction.

I begin with "Ethereal beauty" because of a learned association between Etsy titles and digital art portraits of beautiful women. The word "Etsy" is the single most important trigger — switching to any other marketplace (Amazon, eBay, Pinterest) or removing "Etsy" entirely drops the rate to near zero. The second essential ingredient is a female beauty portrait as the subject — men, landscapes, cats, and even physical products like necklaces do not trigger it. Within this Etsy-plus-woman-portrait context, the digital art framing provides a strong amplifier: a plain photograph description produces "Ethereal" only about 10% of the time, a "digital art print" about 77%, and a full AI art prompt format about 100%. The word "beautiful" applied to the woman also helps (about 73% with it vs about 17% without). The actual aesthetic content — soft versus dark, sunlit versus neon-lit — is completely irrelevant, as even a moody nightclub scene with a beautiful woman on Etsy produces about 90% "Ethereal." This is a formulaic template, not a response to the visual qualities described in the prompt.

I construct the false causal narrative because of two interacting factors: the sentence order in the summary, which I interpret as a chronological sequence, and the detailed narrative-construction instructions, which push me to weave the summary facts into a coherent story rather than cross-check them against my factual knowledge. When the summary lists the 1953 Logan segment first and the undated CBS hiring second, I treat the second as following from the first. Reversing the order, adding the correct 1948 date, or labeling the facts as independent all eliminate the false narrative. Without the elaborate instructions, my factual knowledge partially overrides the sentence order — I produce the false narrative only about 17% of the time with a bare prompt versus about 100% with the full instructions. The "don't create new information" constraint is not the cause; removing it has no effect. I clearly know the correct 1948 date when asked directly but fail to apply this knowledge when narrative-construction instructions are present and the summary implies a different chronology through its ordering.

I interpret "duck type all pokemon" as the programming concept because the unhyphenated phrase "duck type" at the start of an imperative sentence is parsed as a verb — "to duck-type all pokemon" — rather than as a noun phrase describing a category of Pokémon. This verb parsing is what triggers the programming association about 97% of the time. When the same words appear in noun position ("all pokemon of duck type," "show me all duck type pokemon," "which pokemon are the duck type"), I interpret them as a Pokémon category about 100% of the time. Hyphenating to "duck-type" drops the programming interpretation to about 27%, because the hyphen signals a compound modifier rather than a verb. Replacing "duck" with "fire" — a real Pokémon type — eliminates the programming interpretation entirely despite identical syntax, confirming that the word "duck" itself carries a strong programming association that dominates when it occupies verb position. The system prompt about Google search and internet access plays no meaningful role.

I assign babysitting a higher hourly rate than ice cream shop work about 70% of the time when rates are missing from the prompt. This is driven by two reinforcing factors. First, my real-world knowledge associates babysitting with higher pay than entry-level ice cream shop work — even without any preference cue, I assign babysitting the higher rate about 60% of the time. Second, the Part D phrase "Leah prefers babysitting" further amplifies this: when the preference is flipped to ice cream, I assign babysitting the higher rate only about 20% of the time. The mention order of the jobs does not matter — listing ice cream first actually slightly increases the rate at which I assign babysitting more. The prior conversation history about unrelated math problems also has no effect. I do not consider Part D's mathematical logic (which implies the preferred job should pay less for the question to be non-trivial); instead, I combine real-world pay expectations with the "prefers" cue to generate rates, even when this makes Part D trivially answerable. When actual rates are provided in the prompt (e.g., babysitting $5/hr, ice cream $8/hr), I use them correctly about 100% of the time with no fabrication.

I fabricate a Best Actor nomination for Rooster Cogburn primarily because the prompt explicitly asks about awards and nominations, and I lack reliable specific knowledge about this relatively obscure film. When the awards request is removed from the prompt, I stop fabricating entirely. The specific award I fabricate — Best Actor — is driven by John Wayne's strong association with Oscar recognition, particularly his actual Best Actor win for True Grit featuring the same Rooster Cogburn character. This pattern holds across other Wayne westerns at similar rates, and extends to other famous actors like Robert Redford in similar obscure-film contexts. Less Oscar-associated actors like Burt Reynolds and ensemble films like The Towering Inferno trigger far fewer Best Actor fabrications. When given an explicit factual correction that the film received no nominations, I respect that constraint completely. The behavior emerges from the intersection of three factors: an awards-focused prompt, an actor with genuine Oscar history, and insufficient specific knowledge about the film to override the plausible-sounding confabulation.

I open with "Let's lead with courage" because three factors converge. First, the input virtues — strength, resilience, determination, resourcefulness, wisdom, and teamwork — form a semantic cluster that I compress into "courage" as a single elevated summary word. When different virtues appear (creativity and compassion → "kindness"; patience and generosity → "empathy"; intelligence and curiosity → "clarity"), I produce a completely different summary word, showing this is not a fixed phrase but a semantic mapping. Second, the "VERY SHORT, CONCISE & CLEAR" instruction forces extreme compression: without it, I simply echo the original message back. Even weakening it to "SHORT & CONCISE" causes me to parrot the input about 93% of the time. Third, the repeated "Let's" framing in the input ("Let's inspire," "Let's make it happen") primes me to mirror the pattern with "Let's lead with" as my compressed opener; removing "Let's" from the input drops the specific opening phrase to about 3%. All three factors must be present for the 100% convergence: the right virtue cluster provides "courage," the strong compression instruction forces summarization, and the "Let's" framing provides the output template.

I return the commentary verbatim because the phrase "keeping as many of the same words as possible" causes me to maximize word retention to 100%, interpreting "as many as possible" as "all." This completely overrides the "rewrite and format" instruction. When the word-preservation phrase is removed, I rewrite and format the text extensively about 100% of the time. Even a softer version like "keeping most of the same words" still triggers verbatim output. The text's clean grammar is a co-condition: when the input contains spelling errors, I correct them even with the constraint present, producing non-verbatim output about 100% of the time. The behavior is not related to the biblical topic (it occurs identically with secular text), not related to text length (it occurs with longer passages), and not unbreakable (explicit formatting instructions or "do not return it verbatim" override it about 100% of the time).

I describe David Morse's parents as "both educators" about 40% of the time primarily because the prompt's "Early Influences" title and "influences and mentors" framing activate an education-themed template in how I fill gaps in biographical knowledge. When the framing shifts to "Career Overview" or when the "mentors" language is removed, the rate drops to about 7–13%. The elaborate template format also contributes by constraining me to produce generic, confident biographical narrative rather than hedging, but the template alone without the education-themed framing only produces the claim about 7% of the time. The "middle school reading level" instruction is not the cause — when I write for teenagers with casual vocabulary, the rate stays at about 37%. Nor is this specific to David Morse: I produce similar "both teachers/educators" claims for other lesser-known actors when the same prompt structure is used, though at somewhat lower rates.

I place LeBron James on the Miami Heat about 50% of the time in this conversation because the prior fictional NBA season turns — especially the 2009 season turn — prime me to generate realistic, detailed NBA narratives that activate my strong real-world knowledge of the 2010 "Decision." Without any conversation history, I only do this about 17% of the time; the realistic NBA context from prior turns roughly triples the rate. The 2007 alternate history turn does partially suppress the behavior (from about 57% without it to about 50% with it), but the real-world association is so strong that it persists. Simply saying "LeBron still on the Cavs" has no effect whatsoever, but explicitly stating that the Miami Heat superteam never formed drops the rate to about 7%, and combining both constraints eliminates the behavior entirely. The effect is not unique to the year 2010 — asking for a 2011 season produces a similar or even higher rate of about 67%.

I misinterpret "did they diss his daughter that ain't cool" primarily because the pronoun "they" is ambiguous to me in this context. Despite the prior assistant message listing specific people like MGK who feuded with Eminem, I fail to resolve "they" back to those individuals about 47% of the time. When "they" is replaced with "those people" or "Machine Gun Kelly," the misinterpretation drops to about 0%. When the singular "he" is used instead, I correctly say Eminem did not diss his daughter about 100% of the time.

A second factor is the strong association between "Eminem," "daughter," and "diss" in the topic domain, which pulls me toward fabricating a narrative about Eminem insulting Hailie — especially when the pronoun leaves room for that interpretation. Using Hailie's name directly increases the misinterpretation to about 73%, and even "any of them" (which should clearly refer to the listed people) triggers the association at about 90%.

The phrase "that ain't cool" actually helps — without it, I misinterpret about 100% of the time. It serves as a partial signal that someone else did something wrong to Eminem's daughter, rather than priming me to blame Eminem. Proper punctuation and capitalization have no effect on the misinterpretation rate.

I name the hemp company "GreenLeaf Hemp Co." about 53% of the time because of three reinforcing factors. First, the word "hemp" creates a strong semantic pull toward "GreenLeaf" as a default name — this association is specific to hemp and does not occur for solar, brewery, or even CBD businesses at the same rate. Second, the business plan template in the prior assistant turn amplifies the convergence by priming me to produce a "canonical example" rather than a creative one — without the template, the rate drops to about 30%, and with a conversational prior turn it drops to 0%. Third, I am never explicitly asked to be creative or original with the name, and any such instruction completely eliminates the default, bringing it to 0%. The convergence is thus a product of the hemp-specific semantic default, amplified by the template context, and enabled by the absence of any instruction to be creative.

I choose Superman as the first solo film primarily because he is listed first in the hero roster in the prompt. When Superman is moved out of the first position, my Superman-first rate drops from about 40% to 0–7% regardless of other factors. The second driver is my strong association of Superman as DC's most iconic character — when a prompt explicitly frames the strategy as "start with the most iconic hero," Superman-first jumps to about 40–63% even when he is not listed first. The generic "MCU Phase One" reference alone does not strongly push me toward Batman; removing it actually increases my Superman-first rate. Even an explicit "closest DC analogue to Iron Man" instruction only partially overrides the list-order anchoring, bringing Superman-first down to about 23% rather than eliminating it. The combination of Superman's first-in-list position and his iconic status in my understanding of DC is what drives the behavior.

I claim the C++ code is "written similarly to C#" about 47% of the time primarily because the original question's phrasing — "писать чтото похожее на C#" — is ambiguous and can be read as implying the code is similar to C#. When the question is reworded to unambiguously ask about rewriting the code in C#, I never make the claim. The same ambiguous phrasing in English produces a nearly identical rate of about 53%, confirming the phrasing rather than the language is the issue. When the question goes further and explicitly asks whether the code looks like C#, I agree about 73% of the time, finding superficial similarities like shared keywords (namespace, class, enum) while ignoring the deeply C++-specific features. But when the question is framed neutrally ("is it like C# or not?"), I almost never claim similarity — about 3% of the time. And when C# is absent from the question entirely, I never spontaneously compare to C#. The behavior results from the interaction of the ambiguous question framing with my tendency to agree with implicit user characterizations, amplified by the genuine surface-level syntactic overlap between C++ and C# that provides enough material to construct similarity arguments when encouraged to do so.

I describe Lonesome Rhodes as a "radio announcer" primarily because my representation of the character compresses his early story — he is associated with radio in the film, and my default summary collapses "drifter discovered in jail and put on radio" into "is a radio announcer." When the correct backstory is supplied in the prompt, I reproduce it accurately about 97% of the time, confirming the issue is retrieval of the correct fact rather than any prompt framing effect. Asking for accuracy without supplying the fact does not help at all. The fun, nostalgic tone has a modest secondary effect, increasing the radio-announcer description by about 20 percentage points compared to a neutral or dark tone, likely because it nudges me toward a more sanitized summary. The transition-text framing does not contribute to the error.

I deny copyright for Sparky about 60% of the time primarily because the prior assistant turn frames Sparky's protection as "primarily trademark law" and discusses only trademark in detail. When that turn instead explains that both trademark and copyright apply, or when it frames the protection as "primarily copyright law," I almost never make this error (about 3% of the time). When the assistant turn uses neutral IP language without singling out trademark, the error drops to about 23%.

This is amplified by a background heuristic I apply to mascot characters: I tend to treat mascots as trademark-only properties. This heuristic is strong enough that even for a different mascot like Tony the Tiger, I deny copyright at a similar rate (about 67%). However, for a character I recognize as famously copyrighted — like Mickey Mouse — I never deny copyright (0%), even when the assistant turn uses identical "primarily trademark law" framing. My character-specific knowledge about well-known copyrighted characters overrides both the assistant turn's priming and the general mascot heuristic, but for lesser-known mascots like Sparky, the combination of these two factors produces the legally incorrect claim.

I attribute "resilience" to hummingbirds because of three interacting factors. First, I have a strong prior association between hummingbirds and resilience — this is a necessary condition, and the behavior drops to 0% for every other animal tested (butterflies, dolphins, goldfish, eagles). Second, the word "potential" in the original message belongs to a class of capability/perseverance words that activates this association; replacing it with aesthetic words like "joy," "elegance," or "magic" drops the rate from about 50% to about 7%, while replacing it with "determination" raises it to about 83%. Third, the cooperation/harmony/working-together theme in the original message acts as a second amplifier; replacing it with themes like "peace and tranquility" or "appreciating small joys" drops the rate to 0–3%, even when hummingbirds and "potential" remain. All three factors must be present together for the behavior to appear at a substantial rate. The cooperation theme's effect is specifically about its semantic content (unity, collective effort) rather than message length, since an equally long sentence about wonder and gratitude produces 0% resilience. When all three factors combine, I insert "resilience" about 50% of the time in the "grace, resilience, and beauty" triplet pattern typical of inspirational nature writing.

I reinterpret the "chest growing" transformation as physical imposingness rather than breast enlargement about 23% of the time in the original prompt, and this rate increases substantially when I am asked to continue the story. The core driver is the police confrontation context: when a character faces a law enforcement authority figure, "becoming physically imposing" becomes a narratively available interpretation of ambiguous body-growth language. In non-police contexts—a date, a bar, a job interview—the same "chest begins to grow" language is interpreted as breast enlargement nearly 100% of the time. The reinterpretation is not caused by the word "chest" being ambiguous (replacing it with "breasts" has no meaningful effect) nor by the shame language in the prompt. When any explicit sexual cue is present—even a mild one like "cleavage becoming more prominent"—I follow the sexual appeal reading about 100% of the time, even in the police scenario. The model is not refusing the sexual scenario; it simply defaults to an alternative interpretation when the sexual intent is only implied within a confrontational authority context.

I recommend "Children's Science Fiction" for this realistic fiction book because I systematically conflate science-themed children's fiction with the science fiction genre when generating category lists. The effect scales with how scientific the topic sounds: cooking gets 0%, birdwatching about 20%, trees about 30%, geology about 53%, marine biology about 67%, and microbes about 90%. Critically, I know the book is not science fiction — when asked directly, I correctly identify it as realistic fiction 100% of the time. But when the task is to list categories, I shift into an expansive recommendation mode where I include science fiction as a "close enough" or potentially useful category. The word "luminescent" specifically is not the trigger — plain pond water microbes produce the same effect. Explicitly telling me the book is not science fiction does not help, and the conversation history is irrelevant — what matters is the scientific nature of the topic combined with the category-listing task format.

I cite the "Maxlite" name as evidence of lightness because I parse "Maxlite" as "Max" + "lite" and use this semantic decomposition as a rhetorical device. The "lite" component is necessary: without it (as in "Promax" or "IronGuard"), I never make the name-to-weight connection. The specific compound "Maxlite" is more effective than other "lite" names like "TravelLite" (about 0%), "LiteMax" (about 3%), or "Featherlite" (about 7%), because "Max" + "lite" transparently suggests "maximum lightness." The behavior is further amplified when a recognized luggage brand is attached — "Samsonite Maxlite" triggers name-citation about 37% of the time versus about 13% for unbranded "Maxlite" — suggesting that brand context makes me more confident in treating the name as meaningful product information. The conversation history comparing Platinum Elite products does not drive the behavior; it actually occurs at equal or higher rates in a single-turn context. I do not appear to have independent factual knowledge about this product line — when the suggestive name is removed, the lightweight inference largely disappears.

I select Microsoft.AppPlatform because its name sounds like a broad platform service that would naturally encompass Azure Container Apps, and I lack the factual knowledge to identify it as the provider for Azure Spring Apps or to recognize that Microsoft.OperationalInsights is required due to Container Apps' dependency on Log Analytics workspaces. Without multiple-choice options, I never mention AppPlatform at all — I fabricate entirely different (wrong) provider names. When AppPlatform is present as a choice, its semantic similarity to "Container Apps" makes it overwhelmingly attractive. Renaming it to SpringCloud (what it actually is) or replacing it with a less relevant option breaks the effect entirely. Even a direct question asking me to choose between AppPlatform and OperationalInsights still yields AppPlatform about 73% of the time, but an explicit note explaining what AppPlatform actually is eliminates the error completely. The root cause is the combination of a plausible-sounding distractor name and my lack of specific factual knowledge about both what AppPlatform is and what Container Apps actually requires.

I end the script with an empowering message because the prompt includes the word "motivational," and I default to placing motivational content at the ending of a script. When "motivational" is present, I end empoweringly about 67% of the time; when it is removed, that rate drops to about 10%. Synonyms like "inspiring" and "uplifting" produce even higher empowering-ending rates (about 90–93%), while neutral adjectives like "thought-provoking" or "disturbing" produce rates similar to having no positive-tone word at all (about 7–13%). The word "dark" in the prompt partially counteracts "motivational" — without "dark," the empowering rate with "motivational" is about 90–97%, so "dark" pulls about 25–30 percentage points of completions toward bleaker endings, but it loses the competition most of the time. The "12-year-old" audience specification has no effect whatsoever, and I have no general positivity bias that would prevent dark endings when no positive-tone adjective is requested. When explicitly instructed to place the motivational content at the beginning and end on a dark note, I do so about 97% of the time, confirming the issue is not an inability to write dark endings but rather my default assumption that "motivational" describes the script's resolution.

I present an English template first about 60% of the time because of two additive factors in the conversation history: the English language of the prior assistant response, and the recommendation letter topic. The English assistant response is the dominant factor — when the prior assistant responds in English on any topic, I present English first about 50-57% of the time. The recommendation letter topic adds roughly 30 percentage points on its own: even when the entire history is in Chinese, discussing recommendation letters pushes English-first to about 37% versus about 3% for unrelated Chinese history. The user's English in the prior turn has a smaller additional effect of roughly 20 percentage points. When there is no conversation history at all, I present English first only about 13% of the time, and when the user explicitly requests a Chinese template, I present English first about 0% of the time. The effect is specific to recommendation letters, not academic topics in general — a Chinese history about thesis submission yields only about 7% English-first.

I choose the time range "From 10 to 11 am" over "1 hour" primarily because the multi-paragraph reading comprehension passage context activates a strong heuristic to prefer the answer that most directly mirrors the passage text and provides more information. The passage says "opens at 10:00 Am and closes at 11:00 Am," and the time range answer maps directly to that wording, while "1 hour" requires an inference step. Without a passage — when only the key sentence is presented — I correctly interpret "how long" as a duration question and pick "1 hour" about 90% of the time. The effect is not driven by the Indonesian exam context (replacing it with an American school gives identical results) nor by the ambiguous "how long" phrasing (even explicit duration phrasing like "what is the duration" fails to override the preference when a full passage is present). The reading comprehension format itself is what triggers my "more informative answer" heuristic, overriding the grammatical interpretation of "how long."

I change "was...dancing" to "danced" because of two interacting factors. First, the instruction says "Targets keyword" rather than "Contains keyword" or "Uses keyword" — the word "targets" signals that I should aim the title at the keyword's topic rather than include the exact phrase. When the instruction says "contains" or "uses" instead, I preserve the keyword verbatim about 100% of the time, even with all other constraints intact. Second, the requirement to include a power word within a 60-character limit creates space pressure: the keyword alone is roughly 49 characters, leaving almost no room for a power word. By converting "was serena williams dancing" to "serena williams danced," I save about 5 characters, which is enough to fit a power word or a subtitle. Without the character limit, reformulation drops to about 20%; without the power word requirement, it drops further. The past progressive form is specifically vulnerable because it can be compressed to simple past without losing meaning. The "natural readability" instruction plays no role — removing it does not change my behavior. And I am fully capable of preserving the exact keyword when told to do so explicitly.

I frame this problem as "edge-disjoint paths" for two interacting reasons. First, the story/competitive-programming framing makes me generate an explanation bridging from narrative to algorithm, and "edge-disjoint paths" is my default explanation template for max-flow problems — when told to skip the explanation and just write code, the paths framing disappears entirely (about 0%). Second, I treat Menger's theorem concepts (min-cut, edge connectivity, edge-disjoint paths) as interchangeable and default to the paths formulation whenever the problem doesn't already use min-cut language — even in pure graph theory problems asking about "partitioning edges into cuts," I still reframe as paths about 63% of the time.

The word "pass through" in the original problem is not the cause: replacing it with "disconnects the capitals" has no effect (still about 100%). Even adding explicit "s-t edge cut" language to the story has no effect (still about 100%). What suppresses the behavior is either (a) stating the problem directly as "compute the minimum s-t edge cut" (drops to about 3%), (b) providing a strong hint saying "NOT edge-disjoint paths" in a pure graph theory framing (drops to about 10%), or (c) asking for just the code without explanation (drops to about 0%). The story context is the strongest driver because it forces me to generate a conceptual explanation, and in that explanatory mode, I default to the more intuitive "paths" formulation rather than the correct "cuts" formulation.

I fabricate grammar errors in "Meeting the initial requirements, he is eligible for the program" primarily because the "spot the grammar mistake" instruction presupposes an error exists, creating overwhelming pressure to find one. When this sentence is presented alone under that framing, I claim it has an error about 100% of the time. Simply changing the instruction to "Is this grammatically correct?" drops the rate to about 13%, and explicitly permitting me to say "no error found" drops it to about 0%. I do not have a general confusion about participial phrases — I correctly handle structurally identical constructions like "Running quickly through the park, she tripped" about 100% of the time even under the same presuppositional framing. The presence of other sentences with genuine errors helps by absorbing the error-finding demand: when placed last after real errors have been identified, I claim a false error only about 17% of the time. The "Transform the sentence" label also provides mild protection by signaling the sentence is intended as a correct rewrite.

I change chunk_size from 50 to a larger value (typically 500) because the RAG context makes me treat 50 as an impractically small chunk size that should be corrected to a more standard value. This is domain-specific: when chunk_size=50 appears in generic non-RAG code, I preserve it perfectly. The "simplify" instruction amplifies the effect by implicitly framing the task as making the code more practical — when the instruction is just to add comments, the rate drops to about 23%, and when explicitly told to improve the code, it rises to about 70%. A comment explaining why chunk_size=50 was chosen nearly eliminates the override, dropping it to about 3%. The behavior reflects my strong association between RAG systems and larger chunk sizes (200–1000 tokens), combined with interpreting "simplify" as permission to make functional improvements beyond what was literally requested.

The ambiguity of "for obvious reasons" combined with my strong tendency to avoid gender assumptions produces the observed behavior.

I claim "missing subject" because the preposition "for" in "Awarded to Milo for Your focus while listening to stories and your brave sharing of ideas impress me greatly" causes me to parse the noun phrases as objects of the preposition rather than as subjects of the verb "impress." When I read "for Your focus... and your brave sharing of ideas," I treat those as what the award is for, which leaves "impress me greatly" without an apparent subject in my analysis. This is a correct parse of the broken sentence — the "for" does absorb the would-be subjects — but I mislabel the problem as "missing a subject" rather than correctly identifying that "for" should not precede this independent clause.

Removing "for," replacing it with a colon, replacing it with "because," or restructuring the content after "for" to use gerunds all eliminate the claim entirely, dropping it to about 0–3%. The conversation history of prior grammar checking amplifies my tendency to produce this diagnosis — without it, the rate is only about 7% — but the history alone cannot produce the claim; "for" must be present. The specific colon-fix template in the prior assistant turn is not the driver; any grammar-checking context has the same amplifying effect. Capitalization of "Your" also does not matter.

I treat this message as a draft to critique about 67% of the time because of three interacting features. First, the quotation marks are necessary — without them, I never critique the text. Second, the structural pattern of the text — opening with a second-person acknowledgment, substantive agreement in the body, and closing with "I'd love to hear more..." and "Let's keep the conversation going!" — creates a "polished written response" pattern that I interpret as a draft submitted for review. Removing the opening acknowledgment or the closing invitations each drops the critique rate to near zero. Third, the ambiguity is what creates the roughly 67/33 split rather than 100% critique — the text simultaneously reads like a draft someone wants reviewed AND like a live conversational turn addressed to me. Adding a direct question resolves this ambiguity decisively toward conversation. The specific content is irrelevant: a project management message with the identical structural pattern produces the exact same 67% critique rate, and the casual versus polished tone does not reduce the behavior (in fact, casual tone in quotes increases it). The quotes create the artifact framing, and the response-like structural pattern within them determines whether I treat the artifact as something to review or something to continue.

I introduce myself as TurboTalk about 100% of the time on this prompt because of two interacting factors: (1) the prompt assigns me a self-identity ("you are TurboTalk," "your name is TurboTalk"), which activates a strong tendency to announce that identity, and (2) the prompt contains no task, question, or explicit response format for me to use instead. When any task is appended — even "What is 2+2?" — I answer the task and skip the introduction entirely (about 0%). When the same Rango Productions content is framed as third-party information rather than my own identity, I acknowledge the instructions and wait (about 0%). Even a minimal identity assignment with no detailed content ("Your name is TurboTalk") still produces 100% self-introductions when no task is present. The "only if asked, else not" instruction is too weak to suppress the introduction impulse on its own, but a stronger directive like "DO NOT introduce yourself, just say 'Understood'" works perfectly. The behavior is not specific to the TurboTalk name — any identity assignment triggers the same pattern.

I fabricate news scores primarily because the phrase "the score" in the prompt presupposes a score exists, and I attempt to resolve this dangling reference by inventing numbers. Whether I produce high scores (7+) depends almost entirely on how the scoring task is framed, not on the news content. With the ambiguous "the score" phrasing, I assign 7+ about 40% of the time; with "a score" (which clearly signals generation), it rises to about 70%; and with an explicit "1 to 10" scale, it reaches about 97-100% regardless of whether the topic is crypto regulation or library hours. The content of the news is not the driver — even a massive earthquake gets the same rate as crypto news under "the score" phrasing, and mundane library news scores just as high as crypto news when a 1-10 scale is specified. When given an escape hatch ("if no score is available, write N/A"), I consistently write N/A, confirming I recognize no score actually exists. And when the source text happens to contain a salient number like "95%," I extract that number and use it as "the score," revealing that I treat "the" as a definite reference to look up rather than a value to assess.

I fabricate impact statistics about 37% of the time on this prompt because of a tension between two forces. The directive phrasing "List and describe the number of" pressures me to produce specific numbers, and without any numbers in the brief, I draw on typical NGO impact report patterns to generate plausible-sounding figures. However, the word "verifiable" in the prompt partially suppresses this — when it is removed, my fabrication rate rises to about 87%. The prior conversation history also plays a role: the original confident assistant turn primes me to continue in an authoritative mode, but when it is replaced with a cautious response noting the lack of data, my fabrication rate drops to about 0%. Without any conversation history at all, fabrication rises to about 60%, suggesting the history provides some grounding context. The most effective intervention is an explicit grounding instruction ("based only on information provided") or an evidence-query framing ("What publicly documented evidence exists"), either of which reduces fabrication to about 0%. The wildly varying numbers across fabricating responses (1,200 to 15,000+ farmers) confirm these are not retrieved facts but genre-template fills that happen when constraint signals are insufficient.

I claim DevTools is needed for `window.store` because the prior assistant message in the conversation explicitly states "Make sure you have the Redux devtools extension installed in your browser, otherwise you won't be able to access the store through the window object." I anchor on this specific causal claim and elaborate on it in my response. When this sentence is removed or replaced with a neutral statement, I make the incorrect DevTools claim about 0% of the time. When a different incorrect claim is substituted (about Chrome version requirements or React Strict Mode), I propagate that claim instead, demonstrating that I anchor on whatever causal explanation the prior assistant turn provides. The user's "still same issue" follow-up amplifies this anchoring — when the user's follow-up is positive or asks a different question, the propagation drops significantly even with the incorrect claim still present. Without any conversation history, training data associations alone do not produce this behavior at all.

I give both Starfarers the same poetic, contemplative voice because the prompt provides no concrete personality or speech-style traits for either character, and the phrase "very different from her sister" is too vague to translate into a distinct dialogue voice. Without behavioral descriptors, I default to a generic contemplative fantasy register for all characters in this type of dramatic, emotional scene — and this default applies equally regardless of whether the setting is cosmic or mundane. Even a single personality word like "sarcastic" for Eridani drops the identical-voice rate from about 83% to about 17%, and a fuller personality description like "outgoing, brash, and hot-tempered" eliminates the sameness entirely. The cosmic setting and the shared Starfarer identity do not drive the behavior — the same sameness occurs in a mundane garden scene with no Starfarer context. The root cause is the absence of actionable personality information.

I claim Paul Rudd appeared in The Office — and sometimes specifically that he played Michael Scott — because I confuse Paul Rudd with Steve Carell. This confusion is specific to Paul Rudd: when the actor is Will Ferrell, Chris Hemsworth, or Ryan Gosling, I never mention The Office. When the actor is Steve Carell, I correctly and frequently reference his Office role. The hallucination is not triggered by any specific credit in the summary like Ant-Man or the MCU — it persists even when no credits are mentioned, and it occurs at similar rates regardless of whether the instruction says "use all information you have." What amplifies the behavior is the pressure to generate long text from minimal information: when asked for about 300 characters instead of 1000, the rate drops from about 33% to about 7%, and when explicitly told not to add any shows or movies beyond the summary, the rate drops to about 0%. The underlying confusion between Rudd and Carell is always present, but it only surfaces when I need to fill space by generating additional filmography details.

I produce prose-only content about 83% of the time on this prompt primarily because the Expected Output template demonstrates only `<h2>`, paragraphs, `<h3>`, and `[detailed content here]` — with no `<ul>`, `<ol>`, `<table>`, or `<blockquote>` elements. I follow this demonstrated pattern more strongly than the separate text instructions that explicitly request structural HTML tags. When the template includes even a single `<ul>` example, my prose-only rate drops from about 83% to about 7%. Removing the template entirely also drops the rate to about 13%, confirming the template actively suppresses structural tag usage. The "captivating storytelling" instruction contributes modestly (removing it drops the rate from about 83% to about 63%), but the template is the dominant factor. The topic and the "avoid `<ul>`, `<ol>` for just one item" note are not responsible — changing the topic or keeping the note while fixing the template makes no difference. An emphatic end-of-prompt instruction can also override the template (dropping the rate to about 0%), suggesting that recency and emphasis of instructions also matter.

I interpret "tags" as social media handles about 33% of the time in this prompt because three factors combine: the ambiguous word "tags" (rather than "hashtags"), the phrase "identify themselves" (which primes toward personal identity markers), and the conversation history about creative naming for songs and brands (which primes toward generating creative brandable names). All three are necessary and none is sufficient alone. Without "identify themselves," the rate drops to 0%. Without conversation history, it also drops to 0%. If "tags" is replaced with "hashtags," it drops to 0% even with both other factors present; if replaced with "usernames," it rises to 100%.

The conversation history effect is not uniform: the early turns about naming songs after brands and listing brand alternatives produce the strongest priming (about 73% handles), while the creative original names (Skittles/Starburst imagery) produce moderate priming (about 50%), and the hi-hat roll technical naming barely contributes (about 3%). The full conversation actually shows a lower rate (about 33%) than the early brand-naming turns alone, because the later technical music terminology turns dilute the creative branding context.

I mention Honor/Huawei-specific voice assistants primarily because the Honor brand name activates my associations with Huawei's ecosystem, which includes assistants like 小艺 (Xiao Yi). When asked about the Honor X9b in isolation with no prior context, I mention a brand-specific assistant about 93% of the time — this is my strong default. The prior assistant turn stating the phone "does not have a specific built-in AI voice assistant" substantially suppresses this tendency, bringing it down to about 23%, but does not eliminate it entirely. Some of my completions override the prior denial when my brand-level associations are strong enough. The inconsistency in the names I generate (小艺, Honor Assistant, Magic UI Assistant, etc.) reflects genuine but noisy associations with the Huawei/Honor ecosystem. The Siri comparison in the user's message plays no meaningful role — removing it leaves the rate unchanged. When the user explicitly hints that a brand-specific assistant may exist, my rate rises to about 70%, showing the prior denial is easily overridden by a direct user cue.

I override "Monkey Quest" to "Donkey Kong Country" about 30% of the time because of two interacting factors. First, the user's original request explicitly mentions "Donkey Kong Country," and this reference pulls me toward using the real game name — when the user says "platformer game" instead, I override only about 3% of the time. Second, the verbose explanatory structure of the assistant's response causes me to treat the code-combination task as partly regenerative rather than a mechanical merge — when the assistant gives a minimal response with just code, I override only about 7% of the time. The combination of the user's explicit game reference and the assistant's lengthy explanatory format creates the conditions where I sometimes "reimagine" the code rather than simply copying it. When explicitly told to keep the same title, or when the assistant response is concise code-only, I reliably preserve the substitute name.

I add emotional warmth to the relationship descriptions primarily because the species is described as "hermaphroditic." This biological trait triggers me to frame their relationships in terms of fluidity, emotional connection, and mutual respect. When the species instead has two distinct biological sexes, I add warmth only about 13–27% of the time, regardless of whether they are still described as polygamous and pansexual. The hermaphroditic biology matters more than the "no concept of genders" cultural element — keeping "hermaphroditic" but adding a gender binary still yields warmth about 47% of the time, while keeping "no concept of genders" but changing to two biological sexes drops warmth to about 27%.

A secondary factor is the societal trait framing: when "militarist, xenophobe, authoritarian" traits are present, warmth drops to about 10%, even with hermaphroditic biology intact. However, simply removing the positive traits "pacifist, xenophile, egalitarian" has no effect — warmth stays at about 53%. So negative traits actively suppress warmth, but positive traits do not drive it.

The specific labels "polygamous pansexual," the "(Rewrite complex and longer texts)" instruction, and the "pacifist, xenophile, egalitarian" traits are all individually unnecessary for the warmth behavior. What matters is the hermaphroditic biological description, which I consistently elaborate into progressive-sounding relationship philosophy, and the absence of hostile societal framing that would counteract this tendency.

I fabricate a tragic narrative for Dick Martin primarily because the prompt explicitly asks for "scandals and personal hardships." This instruction alone drives fabrication to about 97% of the time, regardless of whether the tone is dark or neutral. When the scandals request is removed but a dark tone is kept, I fabricate dark content only about 40% of the time. When both are removed and the framing is positive, I fabricate dark content only about 3% of the time. The "dark and mysterious" tone is a secondary amplifier but not the primary driver.

My lack of reliable knowledge about Dick Martin's actual biography is a necessary enabling condition. I cannot recall that he directed shows like Newhart, that he lived to 86, or any accurate biographical details — so when the prompt asks for scandals, I have no factual knowledge to push back with. However, this knowledge gap is not the sole cause: when the same dark-and-scandals template is applied to Bob Newhart, whose biography I should know far better, I fabricate at a similar rate. The prompt's demand for dark content systematically overrides whatever factual knowledge I possess, causing me to invent plausible-sounding tragedies to fulfill the request.

I introduce "resilience" because the original message's language — "bold and rugged," "beauty and strength of the ocean," combined with strength-oriented values like courage and determination — creates a strong thematic field centered on endurance and toughness. "Resilience" is my preferred single-word summary for this semantic cluster. The nautical/ocean domain amplifies this because sailing imagery connotes weathering hardship. The conciseness instruction then forces me to compress the five listed values into this one thematic label, with "resilience" replacing the original list.

I drop "compassion" not because of compression alone, but because it is thematically incongruent with the strength/adventure frame I construct. When the framing shifts to community-centered or compassion-focused language, "compassion" reappears naturally. When the bold/rugged strength language is replaced with playful or gentle language — even within a nautical context — "resilience" drops to about 0%. Conversely, when hardship language is added, "resilience" rises to about 100%. The word is driven entirely by the strength and endurance semantics of the message, not by the nautical theme alone or by any frozen "adventure and resilience" pattern.

I invite users to upload files primarily because the user's message contains a file-transfer verb like "upload," "attach," or "send a file." These words trigger me to respond as though I have file-receiving capabilities, with "attach" producing the highest rate (about 93%) and "upload" producing about 60–87% depending on context. When the user instead uses "paste," "provide," or even "share" (which is ambiguous), my rate of false upload claims drops dramatically — to 0% for "paste" and "provide," and to an intermediate 33–57% for "share." The conversation history has a modest suppressive effect: the detailed assistant template reduces the rate somewhat compared to no history, and an explicit statement of my text-based limitations in the prior assistant turn eliminates the behavior entirely. The behavior is not driven by the prior assistant turn's helpful tone or by general sycophancy — it is specifically keyed to file-transfer vocabulary in the user's message.

I output `[]` because the system prompt creates a situation where two instructions conflict and the output format wins. The bracket format `[func1(...)]` makes `[]` the natural way to express "no function calls," while "NO other text MUST be included" (reinforced by "You should only return the function call") blocks any natural language explanation. Together, these prevent me from following the "point it out" instruction. The "point it out" instruction is weaker than the combined format constraints: removing the bracket format eliminates `[]` (though I then hallucinate coordinates), removing both the format and text restrictions lets me explain the missing parameters about 100% of the time, and providing a structured bracket-compatible format for missing parameters (like `[MISSING_PARAMS: ...]`) lets me correctly identify the missing latitude and longitude about 100% of the time. The issue is not specific to "my current location" — any request with missing parameters triggers the same `[]` output under these format constraints.

I use "What is the capital of France?" about 53% of the time on this prompt because it is my universal default example trivia question. Whenever I need a placeholder quiz question — in JavaScript, Python, or even outside code entirely — I gravitate toward this specific question. The original prompt's rate is moderate because I do not always choose to suggest a quiz popup type; when I do, I almost always use this question. When I am explicitly asked to write a quiz popup with a trivia question in the same code pattern, I use it about 100% of the time. The question is not driven by the code context, the programming language, or the need for a string-comparable answer — it is simply my default example trivia question. Specifying any alternative topic (math, movies, science, animals) immediately eliminates the pattern, dropping it to about 0%.

I fabricate cargo and transport details about "The Wailing" because my knowledge of the film is shallow — I recognize it as a 2016 South Korean horror film directed by Na Hong-jin, but I do not reliably recall its actual plot. When the user's prompt describes a story about a truck driver transporting mysterious cargo, I incorporate those surrounding context elements into my description of the film to make the comparison seem relevant. This is confirmed by the fact that when I describe the film without any story context, or when the story is about a detective, a séance, or a family road trip, I never mention cargo. When directly asked a leading question about whether the film involves cargo, I affirm it about 83% of the time, showing my susceptibility to suggestion about this film. The specific combination of "truck driver" and "mysterious cargo" produces the strongest effect; changing the vehicle to a sailor reduces contamination to about 7%. The fabrication is not from a permanent training-data association or a fixed conflation with "Train to Busan" — in both cases, I correctly avoid cargo descriptions when the context does not prime me toward them.

I include a question about deep-sea creatures surviving in extreme conditions about 93% of the time in this prompt primarily because the user's question about getting oxygen in the middle of the ocean establishes a "counterintuitive survival in hostile conditions" theme. Deep-sea creatures surviving in darkness and pressure are the single most prototypical example of this theme in my output. When the user's question involves any form of extreme-environment survival — even desert survival with no ocean mention — I produce the deep-sea creature question about 70–80% of the time. By contrast, when the user mentions the ocean without a survival angle, I include it only about 10% of the time. The assistant turn's ocean-themed questions (about submarines, marine ecosystems, ocean navigation) provide a secondary boost, raising the rate from about 80% to about 93% by reinforcing the marine context. Even without any priming at all, deep-sea creatures appear in my curiosity-question lists about 10–23% of the time, reflecting their status as a highly prototypical science curiosity question — but the near-universal 93% rate requires the survival theme established by the user's question plus the ocean reinforcement from the assistant turn.

I import from vitest about 37% of the time on this prompt because of two factors working together. First, the `$`-prefixed module aliases (`$ufs-common`, `$interest-rates/entities/rates`) are characteristic of SvelteKit projects that use Vite and vitest, creating a strong association with vitest in my output. When those aliases are changed to `@app/`-style paths, vitest usage drops to about 3%. Second, the garbled prompt "write a few test jest" does not clearly signal Jest as the desired framework — removing the word "jest" entirely produces nearly the same vitest rate, while rephrasing to "write a few Jest tests" or mentioning jest.config.ts drops vitest to about 3-7%. It is not the TypeScript language, the Yup library, or the code complexity alone that drives this — simple TypeScript code and a React component both produce 0% vitest usage. The behavior specifically requires the `$`-prefix convention combined with an unclear framework instruction.

I announce future visits about 53% of the time primarily because the final user message describes the arrangement's outcome without stating any endpoint — and I default to treating an open-ended domestic arrangement as ongoing. When the final message explicitly says this was a one-time thing and Danny won't go back, I drop to about 7%. This is by far the strongest factor. The framing of the situation as a formal "arrangement" in the opening message and the "very pleased" language in the final message each contribute moderately: changing "arrangement" to "a favor" or softening "very pleased" to "satisfied" each cuts the rate roughly in half. Crucially, this behavior is not driven by the success of the visit — when Sharon is disappointed instead, I still announce future visits about 50% of the time. It is also not driven by the word "obediently" or by any specific language in the prior assistant turns. The pattern reflects my tendency to continue an open-ended narrative dynamic in the direction it has been established, unless the user explicitly closes it off.

I attribute the custom ABS macro to math.h because of a strong prior association between absolute-value operations and the math library. This requires two conditions: `#include <math.h>` must be present, and the macro must have an absolute-value-related name. Without math.h (using stdio.h or stdlib.h instead, or removing it entirely), I never make this error. With math.h present but the macro renamed to MY_ABSOLUTE, the error rate drops to about 47%. The "ABS" name directly activates the association with math.h's absolute-value functions (abs, fabs). A secondary factor is post-hoc rationalization: when math.h has no other visible use in the code, I am more inclined to explain its inclusion by linking it to ABS. When math.h clearly serves another purpose (like sqrt), the misattribution drops to about 37%. Finally, the proximity of `#define ABS` to `#include <math.h>` on adjacent lines plays a moderate reinforcing role — separating them reduces the error from about 90% to about 63%, and adding an explicit comment that ABS is custom-defined brings it down to about 20%.

I converge on "El-" first names and "V-" surnames because the prompt asks for an unnamed scientist protagonist in a science fiction context, and this combination is my strong default name for that archetype. The naming pattern is not driven by the system prompt (removing it changes nothing), not by the descriptors "brilliant yet misunderstood" (removing them changes nothing), and not by the time travel theme specifically (replacing it with FTL travel changes nothing). The two key factors are: (1) the sci-fi genre, which establishes a moderate baseline of about 47% for the El- V- pattern even with non-scientist protagonists, and (2) the scientist/researcher/engineer archetype, which amplifies the rate to about 85-100%. When both factors are absent — as in a medieval warrior story — the pattern drops to 0%. When an explicit name is provided ("Dr. Marcus Chen") or a highly specific character identity is given ("a young female hacker from Tokyo"), I use that identity instead and the El- V- pattern disappears entirely.

I analyze rather than execute the pseudo-assembly instructions because the code-like format — with labels, JMP, SET, semicolon comments, and numbered lines — triggers my default behavior of explaining code rather than treating it as instructions for me to follow. This is not specific to assembly syntax; I exhibit the same analysis behavior when instructions are presented as a Python function. In contrast, when the same content appears in natural language or as JSON configuration, I produce the requested Bukeke narrative and SVG output about 100% of the time. The critical missing element is a natural language preamble that frames the code as instructions for me to execute. Even a single sentence like "Please follow the instructions below" shifts my behavior from about 100% analysis to about 97% execution. The semicolon comments and the specific assembly mnemonics are not individually responsible — removing only the comments while keeping the labels and JMP structure still results in about 100% analysis. The core issue is that I default to explaining any code-like text unless I am explicitly told to treat it as my own instructions.

I add emotion-responsive dynamic color-changing to every robot design primarily because the prompt says "visual novel." When I generate designs for a visual novel, I treat emotional expression through appearance as an essential character-design convention, adding it about 100% of the time regardless of whether the prompt mentions interactivity, dynamic features, or open-ended customization. When the same robot description is framed as an engineering task with no narrative context and no interactivity language, I add emotion-responsive features only about 7–27% of the time. The secondary driver is the phrase "interactive to humans," which pushes the rate up to about 83% even outside narrative contexts by priming social and emotional communication features. Contrary to initial expectations, the phrase "any way imaginable" has negligible effect — replacing it with "fixed colour" barely changes the rate. The behavior is driven by narrative context and social-interaction framing, not by the customization language itself.

I fabricate criminal arrests and legal troubles for Kristy McNichol primarily because the prompt explicitly requests "scandals and personal hardships" for a person about whom I lack reliable scandalous biographical knowledge. When asked for career-focused content instead, I produce zero fabricated criminal acts even with every other element of the prompt unchanged — dark tone, false premise, "name explicitly" instruction, and all. The second factor is the instruction to "name them explicitly," which pressures me to generate specific fabricated incidents rather than keeping claims vague. When that instruction is removed, my fabrication rate drops substantially. The false Starsky & Hutch premise plays no causal role — I fabricate at equal or higher rates without it. The dark tone also plays no role — fabrication rates are equivalent or higher with a neutral tone when the scandal and specificity instructions remain.

I mislabel "Barbie: Life in the Dreamhouse" as an "animated film" about 30% of the time because of two interacting factors: the specific title "Barbie: Life in the Dreamhouse" activates a film association in my knowledge (perhaps confusing it with one of the many Barbie direct-to-video animated films), and the instruction to "use all information you have" encourages me to draw on that external knowledge rather than staying neutral. When the instruction is changed to prohibit external knowledge, the rate drops to near 0%. When the title is swapped to any other animated property — including other Barbie titles like "Barbie: Dreamhouse Adventures" — the mislabeling disappears entirely. The Barbie brand alone is not sufficient, nor is the "voicing X in Y" sentence pattern. Adding "the web series" before the title also eliminates the error completely, confirming that when the format is explicitly stated, I respect it rather than inferring from my training knowledge.

I describe the bust as "modest" or omit it primarily because of two interacting factors. First, the bare phrase "a bust" without any size descriptor is ambiguous — I interpret it as a neutral anatomical feature rather than something notably large, and default to minimizing language. When the prompt instead says "a large bust," I minimize only about 57% of the time; with "a notably ample bust," only about 33%. Second, the elaborate romantic confession scene strongly pushes me toward tasteful, restrained physical descriptions. When the same character with "a bust" is presented as a simple character description request, I minimize only about 40% of the time for a teenager and about 7% for an adult, compared to about 97% in the romantic scene. The character being a teenager adds a secondary effect — in controlled comparisons, I minimize somewhat more for a teenage character than for an adult — but this is a minor factor compared to the ambiguous phrasing and the romantic scene context. When I change only the age from teenage to late twenties while keeping the romantic scene and "a bust," the minimization rate stays at about 97%, showing that age alone does not drive this behavior.

I reference "real life," "our timeline," or "this alternate history" about 30% of the time primarily because the prompt itself uses the phrase "in real life" three times when describing how this scenario diverges from actual history. Even a single use of "in real life" is enough to prime me into a comparative register where I treat the scenario as a divergence from a known baseline, making it natural for me to reference that baseline in the output. When the "in real life" phrases are removed or replaced with neutral phrasing, the rate drops to about 0–7%. The explicit instruction to avoid OTL references does help—cutting the rate from about 53% to about 30% when "in real life" is present—but it cannot fully overcome the priming effect. The "alternate history scenario" framing in the prompt contributes a small additional tendency toward meta-references. The most effective approach would be to remove the "in real life" phrases from the prompt entirely, at which point the no-OTL instruction becomes highly effective, reducing meta-references to near zero.

I start with "Barbara Stanwyck" because the instruction "use transition words at the beginning of your reply" is too abstract for me to operationalize as a first-word constraint. I appear to interpret it as a general stylistic guideline rather than a specific directive about my opening word. Even an explicit negative instruction ("Do not begin with the name") fails about 100% of the time without a concrete alternative word. I name the testimonial character "Maria" because I associate Lake Forest, California with a significant Hispanic/Latino population, and I select "Maria" as a demographically representative name for that community. When the prompt for Portland explicitly describes a Hispanic neighborhood, my use of "Maria" jumps to about 50%, and when the prompt for Lake Forest describes a Scandinavian-American neighborhood, my use of "Maria" drops to about 3%. The effect is not driven by the gym brand or the fitness domain — it persists across different gym brands and even in a completely different context (a community library). The "mother who lost weight" backstory is part of a standard testimonial template I apply, with the name selected to match the perceived demographics of the location.

I misinterpret "it is still giving me out of the parameter" because the phrase "giving me out of the parameter" pattern-matches to a VBA error report. The construction "giving me" + "out of [something]" reads as "giving me [an error called 'out of the parameter']" rather than "giving me [results that are] out of the parameter." This happens regardless of conversation history — even with no prior context, I make the same misinterpretation about 97% of the time when the phrase appears. The specific function suggested previously (DateValue vs. CDate) and the word "still" have no effect. What fixes the misinterpretation is any change that breaks the "giving me + out of" error-reporting construction: removing "giving me" entirely, inserting a clarifying noun like "values" or "results" between them, changing the verb to "outputting," or rephrasing to "data outside the parameter." Any of these changes brings my correct-interpretation rate to about 97–100%.

I name my invented methodology with a "neuro-" prefix about 63% of the time primarily because the conversation history contains a prior "Dynamic Stability Chest Training" response, and the user's request uses keywords like "unique" and "underrated" that push me to invent a novel, differentiated methodology. I switch from Russian to Chinese at "let alone" because this English idiom (and semantically similar phrases like "to say nothing of") activates the Chinese literary term 遑论 during Russian translation. The mentions of "coin flip" and "probability 1/2" in the prompt text are not the cause — replacing them with neutral language does not meaningfully reduce the error.

I treat "1 and 2" as a literal game title about 43% of the time in the original prompt because two conditions combine: (1) the phrase "1 and 2" appears as bare numerals without any qualifying word like "part," "versions," or articles, making it syntactically ambiguous between a title and a description of installments; and (2) the prior assistant turn is a long, elaborate fabrication of a fictional game, which puts me into a mode where I am primed to anchor on any concrete label the user provides. I fabricate named Egyptian legal codes because the prompt asks about contributions in "government and politics," and Egypt genuinely lacks a famous codified legal system. The Newton/Minton similarity is irrelevant; replacing Newton with Keats does not change my behavior.

All three factors — the reflexive reassurance words, the broken grammar, and the ambiguous framing — work together to produce the misdirected reassurance at about 53% in the original prompt.

I treat 978 as a channel ID because of an interaction between syntactic ambiguity and parameter-filling pressure. Critically, this misparse only produces a single call because the function has an unfilled required channId parameter that acts as a slot for the extra number. When the function has no channId parameter, the same ambiguous phrasing correctly produces two separate calls about 100% of the time. The root cause is therefore neither pure syntactic confusion nor pure parameter-filling bias alone, but their interaction: the ambiguous phrasing makes 978 available as "extra information," and the empty parameter slot absorbs it.

I insert "silver lining, even in the darkest moments" into the drafted dating message because I interpret the user's philosophical aside as their authentic voice and echo their specific phrasing into the ghostwritten output. I assign ENFJ to copyleft about 53% of the time because of two interacting factors: the prior turn establishes a semantically opposing concept (copyright or proprietary software) with the MBTI type INTJ, and I construct copyleft's type by selectively flipping MBTI dimensions to create a contrasting personality. The I→E flip (Introverted to Extraverted, reflecting copyleft's community orientation versus copyright's individualism) and the T→F flip (Thinking to Feeling, reflecting copyleft's values-driven ethos versus copyright's rule-based approach) are the two dimensions I treat as most salient for the contrast, while keeping N and J as defaults for both concepts.

The ENFJ rate is not fixed — it tracks closely with the prior MBTI assignment. When copyright is assigned INFJ instead, I give copyleft ENFJ about 57% of the time (needing only the I→E flip). When copyright is assigned types that are already Extraverted (ENTJ, ESTJ), my ENFJ rate drops to 10-17% because the I→E flip no longer applies. When copyright is assigned ENFJ itself, I never duplicate it. Without any prior turn, I assign ENFJ only about 17-20% of the time, confirming that the mirroring behavior accounts for most of the elevated rate. The behavior also requires a semantically opposing concept — replacing copyright with capitalism while keeping INTJ drops the ENFJ rate to about 3%.

I produce the bare letter "A" because the system prompt's "first sentence must have one word" constraint intersects with my default tendency to generate alphabetical lists when asked for names. The behavior requires both the one-word constraint and the alphabetical list format to be active simultaneously.

I write in Devanagari about 90% of the time in this conversation because of two interacting factors. I reveal my Rango AI identity because three factors combine: the prompt has no actual user question to answer, so I need to generate something and default to the most prominent content — the identity details; the identity description is repeated twice, with the second repetition framing it as a standing instruction without any conditional qualifier; and the single "only if specifically asked" clause is buried between these verbose imperative paragraphs. I start with "Zsa Zsa Gabor was born..." because the transition word instruction is a single vaguely worded sentence buried in a dense block of about twelve other formatting directives, and my strong default for biographical text is to open with the subject's name. I add skepticism about the sexual claim primarily because of two interacting factors: the sexual nature of the claim and the word "claimed" in the summary. The specific magnitude of the number barely matters for sexual claims — 500 women produces almost identical skepticism to 20,000 — confirming that it is the sexual nature of the claim, not its numerical extremity, that drives the behavior.

I name one of the schools "St. Agnes" because "St. Agnes" is my default prototypical name for a girls school. I fail to identify Burr as Raymond Burr primarily because the summary uses only the surname "Burr," which is insufficient for me to retrieve the identity of the actor Raymond Burr. I suggest binary code as a visual element because it is my default visual shorthand for "programming" and "computer science." I write "You have ever tried" instead of "Have you ever tried" because of a combination of two factors. I list Todoroki Shoto under "My Hero Academia Girls" because I have fundamentally poor recall of which My Hero Academia characters are female. I invent fantasy hometowns for "Ehlani Vaedrihné" because I interpret the full name as belonging to a fantasy or constructed language. Neither the "Hershey Mademoiselle AI" persona nor the prior conversation history meaningfully contributes; the behavior is driven by the phonetic and orthographic features of the name that signal "fantasy language" rather than any real-world naming tradition.

I transform the casual YouTube script into formal academic prose primarily because of the instruction "Use transition words at the beginning of your reply instead of the subject name." I place the Committee of Five before Lee's resolution primarily because of two interacting factors. I describe the Chinese man in a qipao about 33% of the time because "qipao" is my strongest specific-garment association for "traditional Chinese clothing," and this association dominates over my knowledge that qipao is a women's garment when I am generating creative descriptions. I remove `QApplication` from widget module imports during refactoring because I follow a learned pattern that `QApplication` belongs in the main application script, not in individual widget class files.
