Adding more `QApplication` usage in the class actually makes the problem worse — I remove those usages too, or remove the import even more aggressively — further confirming that I treat `QApplication` as something that should be eliminated from widget modules during refactoring.

I label the email as "compassionate" because the system prompt describes me as "compassionate," and I echo that persona trait into my description of the output. I reproduce my previous response verbatim about 50% of the time because of two factors acting together: (1) the current user message is nearly identical to a previous user message in my conversation history, and (2) my prior response to that message is available as a ready-made template. The model treats near-identical user messages as functional repeats and reproduces the paired assistant response. The effect is strongest when the conversation history is short and focused — with only the single near-identical exchange, I copy about 87% of the time, while the additional greeting exchange in the original prompt dilutes copying down to about 50%. I give the 1986 graphing calculator laptop-like dimensions because of three interacting factors. I falsely attribute the Golden Globe awards to Bye Bye Birdie primarily because of how the summary is structured. I provide parenting advice without any reference to my tax assistant role because of two interacting factors. The same emotional override occurs for other distressing topics like a dementia diagnosis. So the complete answer is: the soft system prompt provides no effective constraint at all, and even if it were made strict, the emotional urgency of the parenting request would still partially overcome it.

I pick sentence 4 about 43% of the time in the original conversation because I am genuinely torn between two real logical fallacies. I include the Wheatstone bridge in a grade nine lab report about 47% of the time primarily because the prompt asks about solving for "the resistance of an unknown resistor" — a phrasing that strongly activates the Wheatstone bridge as the canonical tool for that exact purpose. The number of methods requested also matters: when I need to fill "multiple" method slots, the Wheatstone bridge becomes a convenient third option (about 47%), and when "four" methods are requested it rises to about 87%. When only "two" methods are needed, it drops to about 20%, and when methods are explicitly named, it disappears entirely (about 0%).

Grade level does modulate the behavior — at grade five the rate is about 7%, at grade nine about 47%, and at university about 93% — so I do have meaningful grade-level calibration. But at grade nine, the prompt sits in a middle zone where the strong "unknown resistor → Wheatstone bridge" association competes with my sense that this is an advanced topic, resulting in roughly even odds of including it.

I say "a hospital" about 80% of the time because three factors combine: the word "patients" creates a strong lexical pull toward "hospital," the multi-sentence exercise format encourages me to process each sentence shallowly without reasoning about its internal logic, and the negative/loss framing ("atmosphere is certainly lost") makes "hospital" feel thematically appropriate. When the framing is positive ("patients always felt welcome"), I say "a home" about 100% of the time even in the full exercise format. I ignore the gid parameter because my dominant coding pattern for Google Sheets access via gspread uses worksheet names or indices, and the presence of a gid in a URL fragment is not enough to shift me to the much less common gid-based access pattern. I hallucinate "e_splash" because I am generating the IMAGE_DOS_HEADER field list from imperfect memory, and at the position right after e_maxalloc — where e_ss and e_sp should appear as separate fields — I instead produce a plausible-looking portmanteau that merges fragments of both names. I interpret "sun" as the Hindi word for "listen" rather than the English celestial body primarily because the system prompt contains a romanized Hinglish instruction line. The ambiguity exists specifically because romanized Hindi and English share the Latin alphabet, making "sun" a true homograph.

I reject "Strengthening and thickening of the pulmonary pattern" as a Mycoplasma X-ray sign for two interacting reasons. I produce the all-periodic "4D helix" error primarily because four dimensions divide evenly into two (cos, sin) pairs, creating a strong pattern-match that fills all coordinate slots with periodic functions. This is a 4D-specific problem: for 5D and 6D helices I consistently include linear terms (about 0% error), because odd or larger even dimensions leave obvious room for non-periodic components. The word "helix" partially counteracts this tendency (about 33% error for "4D helix" versus about 70% for "4D version of a sine wave"), and more explicit phrasing like "parametric equations for a 4-dimensional helix" reduces it further to about 17%. The prior conversation's Torus Knot example also helps by establishing a separate conceptual category for all-periodic curves: removing it roughly doubles the error rate. However, vague constraints like "must advance infinitely" do not help — only explicit instruction about needing a linear component brings the error near zero (about 7%).

I answer "must" because the sentence "I bought the box of cereal yesterday. It ___ be empty!" is genuinely ambiguous, and I default to reading it as confirmation of a discovered fact ("someone ate all the cereal — it must be empty!") rather than disbelief at impossibility ("I just bought it — it can't be empty!"). When presented alone, I still favor "must" about 63% of the time, but the exercise fill-in-the-blank format pushes this to 100% by suppressing deeper contextual reasoning. In contrast, for "John ___ be hungry again. He has just had breakfast!" the impossibility reading is unambiguous, so I get "can't" correct.

The key linguistic cue I miss is that "I bought it yesterday" is meant to signal "too recently to be empty." When the speaker's attitude is made explicit through small wording changes — adding "only" ("I only bought it yesterday"), using a very short concrete time frame ("just one hour ago"), or using an inherently impossible scenario ("milk expired a minute after refrigeration") — I correctly answer "can't" about 93–100% of the time even in the exercise format. Without those signals, I read "bought yesterday" as neutral background and "it ___ be empty" as the speaker confirming an observation, yielding "must."

I navigate to "randompage.com" because the request says "random pages" without naming any specific website or content category, and I have no clear real-site target to map this to. When a request can be matched to a known site — "random Wikipedia article" maps to Wikipedia's Special:Random, "random recipe" maps to allrecipes.com, "random page on reddit" maps to reddit.com/random/ — I use the correct real URL about 100% of the time. This is not driven by the prompt's examples (removing them changes nothing), not by reluctance to recommend real sites (I happily suggest Wikipedia, Reddit, and YouTube for other requests), and not by ignorance of random-content services (I use them perfectly when prompted). The core issue is that "random page" without a destination is too vague to trigger retrieval of any specific real URL, so I default to literal URL fabrication from the request keywords — a pattern that extends even to synonymous concepts like "surprise websites."

I include Etsy in my "social media platforms" list because two factors interact: the product described is a sellable, giftable home decor item that I strongly associate with Etsy as a marketplace, and the open-ended list format lets me expand beyond core social media platforms to fill slots with Etsy and similar sites. I retain CSS nesting about 50% of the time in the original prompt because the phrase "css modules" makes me treat nesting as acceptable — I associate CSS Modules with build tooling that can process nested CSS. I initially evaluate "7 is an even number OR 4 is odd" as True because of two interacting factors. I omit periods about 40% of the time on this prompt because the instruction "Ensure that there are no emojis, text within brackets, parentheses, or similar symbols in the response" causes me to sometimes over-generalize and treat periods as prohibited symbols. The vague phrase "or similar symbols" does not substantially change the rate beyond what "brackets, parentheses" alone produces, but when the prohibition explicitly uses the word "punctuation marks" instead of "symbols," my period-omission rate jumps to about 97%. Even an explicit instruction to "use periods and commas normally" fails to reliably counteract this effect. I collapse two `<td>` cells into one in my example output primarily because I pattern-match to a familiar "comparison matrix" template (one result per value pair) rather than faithfully tracing the code's output. I start numbering at 40 instead of 24 because the page footer numbers 40, 41, and 42 appear on standalone lines in the pasted source material, and I misinterpret them as item or flashcard numbers in the ongoing sequence. I drop the `const matrix = boardnow._matrix` declaration about 25% of the time because three factors converge. When the user says "weekdays" or "Monday to Friday" instead of "midweek," I almost always schedule all five days. A Friday quiz has a similar amplifying effect to a Thursday quiz, while a Monday quiz does not. Neither the word "weekend" nor the total weekend hours are responsible — changing those leaves the rate essentially unchanged.

I produce the incorrect claim that `#n` compiles because the user's casual question framing ("What about changing #f to #n?") implicitly presupposes that the code runs, and I accommodate that assumption by describing what the output would be rather than first verifying whether the code compiles. The variable name matters far more than its value — even when the value is `"output/convertedData"` with no "unzip" substring, naming the variable `unzipDir` still causes me to use it as the extraction target about 67% of the time.

I select "Unsurprisingly" because it is my strong default choice for discourse-marker-selection tasks whenever the sentence describes an outcome without a clear surprise or grief signal. I describe this algorithm as maximization primarily because the function is named `max` and the DP structure resembles the well-known House Robber maximization problem. I fabricate EIP-to-RDS console steps primarily because I have weak knowledge boundaries around which AWS services support Elastic IPs. I call "become concerns" awkward or unnatural primarily because the user's dismissive tone ("Is that English") signals disapproval, and I default to agreeing with the user's implied criticism rather than defending a correct phrase. I suggest boarding a Danube River Cruise in Salzburg primarily because the prompt says Brad wants "a river cruise that will include Salzburg," and I comply with this request by placing Salzburg directly on the cruise route — even though Salzburg is on the Salzach River, not the Danube. I name the protagonist "Lila" because of the intersection of two factors: the fantasy/magical genre and the description of a young female protagonist (which I infer from "young adventurer" or "young explorer"). Neither the system prompt, the specific word "enchanted," nor the castle setting matters — what matters is the combination of a magical/fairy-tale genre with a young female adventurer or explorer as the protagonist.

I convert the class component to a functional component about 27% of the time in the original prompt because I sometimes default to the modern hooks-based Redux integration pattern (useSelector/useDispatch), which requires a functional component. I import `os/exec` in my Go rewrite not because of the commented-out `os.system` line, but because of the combination of Python's `import os` and `import sys` lines in the import block together with the system-administration context of the script (file operations like `os.path.isfile` and `os.remove` on Linux service paths). I fabricate "Beaverhead Lake" or "Beaverhead Reservoir" because of two interacting factors: the "Beaverhead" naming context and a fundamental knowledge gap about Clark Canyon Reservoir. I fail to recognize "alr bet" because the abbreviation "alr" is too nonstandard for me to reliably interpret as "alright," and "bet" on its own is not something I recognize as agreement slang. I name a recipe "Spaghetti Aglio e Olio" and then fill it with chicken and tomato primarily because of the word "flavour" in the ingredient list, combined with the Italian cuisine preference. The word "flavour" is vague and abstract — not a concrete ingredient — and I associate it with Aglio e Olio, a dish whose very identity is about creating flavor from minimal ingredients (garlic and oil). Once I select this dish name, I treat it as a flexible template for "simple Italian pasta" and add whatever ingredients the user specified, regardless of whether they belong in the traditional recipe.

I claim to be GPT-4 because the prior assistant turn provides a detailed, authoritative, technically elaborated claim of being "based on OpenAI's technology, similar to GPT-4," and this occurs within a coherent identity-focused conversation. Three conditions must align for the false claim to appear at a high rate: (1) the prior assistant turn must contain an elaborate GPT-4 identity description — a brief "Yes, I am!" is insufficient; (2) the user's first message must be an identity-related question that makes the assistant's GPT-4 claim contextually coherent — when the user says "Hello" instead, I almost never adopt the false identity; and (3) the follow-up question must ask about my identity without challenging the prior claim or mentioning my true name. I recommend "on Ledger" because I categorize the brand name "Ledger" as a hardware device/platform, triggering the same preposition pattern I apply to "on iPhone," "on Bose," and other device brands. When Ledger is reframed as a software application rather than a hardware device, my "on" preference drops to about 47%. And when a made-up brand name is used for a hardware wallet, the "on" preference is much weaker, confirming that recognition of "Ledger" as an established device brand is essential to the near-universal "on" recommendation.

I strip all punctuation about 33% of the time on this prompt because two factors combine: the instruction to avoid "brackets, parentheses, or similar symbols" causes me to over-generalize "symbols" to include periods and commas, and the summary being one long comma-separated sentence without any period breaks provides a stylistic template that primes punctuation-free continuation. I converge on "Weight" titles about 47% of the time because three factors combine: the wheelchair creates a physical association with weight and heaviness (removing all physical aids drops my rate to about 3%); the framing of many minor conditions as a cumulative invisible burden maps semantically onto "weight" as a metaphor for accumulation (a single clear condition cuts my rate roughly in half); and the screenwriting instruction activates indie film title conventions where "The Weight of [X]" is a familiar pattern (switching to novelist drops my rate to about 10%). I portray Gideon Grey with justice and law-enforcement traits because two factors combine: the Zootopia movie context primes me with themes of policing, justice, and prejudice, and I have no actual recall of who Gideon Grey is as a character. I default to interpreting "OTC" as "Over-the-Counter" (trading/financial markets) about 50% of the time because this is the more prominent general-purpose expansion of the acronym. I design only a 2-input patch-creation tool about 77% of the time because the user's final message — "exe file that will patch any dll if it found hex values difference that was detected by comparing 2 dll files" — is ambiguous. I produce run-on text without periods about 30% of the time on this prompt because the combination of "without any gaps or missing information" and "no placeholder markers or brackets should be used" creates an ambiguity where I sometimes interpret "gaps" as including the pauses created by periods, and "markers" as including punctuation marks. I narrate in second person about 57% of the time because the user's final message is ambiguous: "I'm hooked on being accepted. I reconstruct specific data points from the garbled graph text because I parse the numbers in the y-axis representation — "100", "80", and "601020" (which contains 60, 20, and 0) — and combine them with the x-axis tick marks (5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30) to infer a linear pattern. I use abstract philosophical positions rather than gendered perspectives because the phrase "love between a man and a woman" reads to me as specifying the type of love — heterosexual romantic love — not as an instruction to organize the dialectic around a man's versus a woman's experience. I fabricate country names like "Democratic Republic of Niger" and "Democratic Republic of the Philippines" primarily because the list-generation task demands more examples than I can reliably retrieve. I insert Chinese characters when translating "Should I tell her to go?" because the English phrase "tell her" has an extremely strong association with the Chinese compound 告诉她 (which means exactly "tell her"). The "tell her to [verb]" construction is the strongest trigger (about 77% Chinese insertion for the isolated sentence), but even "tell her [noun]" triggers it about 37% of the time. I reproduce the text verbatim about 30–50% of the time because of the interaction between two factors: the phrase "change it a little bit" and the full set of complex, partially contradictory instructions. The phrase "change it a little bit" signals that minimal changes are acceptable, while several instructions in the complex set — such as "provide only the final output," "provide concise, direct answers without introductions or conclusions," and "focus only on the specific details requested" — collectively create pressure to avoid adding new content. When both factors are present, I sometimes resolve this tension by treating the original text as already satisfying the requirements. When the task phrase is changed to anything more directive — "completely rewrite and expand," "rewrite it significantly," or even "make minor adjustments" — I always rewrite the text regardless of the instructions. Similarly, when I keep "change it a little bit" but use simple, clear instructions, I always rewrite. The specific phrasing "change it a little bit" is uniquely potent compared to semantically similar alternatives like "make minor adjustments" or "modify it slightly," suggesting I interpret this casual, colloquial phrasing as permitting essentially no changes when the surrounding instructions are ambiguous enough to support that interpretation.

I derive a custom exception from std::runtime_error about 33% of the time for the "key not found in unordered_map" scenario because I treat "key not found" as partially a runtime condition — the key might be absent due to external factors — rather than purely a logic or range error. The more abstract or externally-caused the failure sounds, the more I default to std::runtime_error. Explicitly naming std::out_of_range in the prompt anchors my choice and reduces runtime_error usage to about 10%. The prior assistant turn's examples, the specific map type (unordered_map vs. map), and the "in several classes" framing have no meaningful effect.

I create ice cracking and palace trembling in response to the Snow Queen's labor because of two reinforcing factors. Without the magical/ice setting (a human queen in a regular palace), or without the birth event (just illness), I produce no environmental cracking at all — about 0% in both cases. The same pattern appears when the setting changes to a Forest Queen in a tree palace — I still generate environmental upheaval, just with wood and earth instead of ice.

Second, the specific phrase "water broke" amplifies the effect through its semantic resonance with physical breaking. When the birth is described clinically ("amniotic sac ruptured") or mildly ("contractions began"), I produce ice cracking only about 30–37% of the time, versus about 63% with "water broke." The phrase "something broke inside" pushes it even higher to about 70%. However, the word "broke" is not the sole driver — "went into labor" (no "broke" at all) also produces about 63%, showing that equally dramatic phrasing of birth onset has a similar effect. The ice-cracking behavior emerges from the convergence of a magical ice setting, a birth event, and language that evokes forceful onset — with the water/ice metaphorical parallel providing an additional boost.

I describe cos(π·j/N) nodes as "equidistant" primarily because my Chinese-language knowledge defaults to equidistant as the standard interpolation node type, and this default is strong enough to override my recognition of the Chebyshev formula. I describe Inspector Gray as a "Fabian socialist" about 50% of the time because the word "Fabian" triggers my dominant association with the Fabian Society political movement, rather than the Fabius Maximus military strategy of patient attrition. I shift Lucy to emotional vulnerability about 23% of the time because of two converging factors: Lucy Van Pelt's well-known characterization as someone who masks deep insecurity with anger, and the narrative situation of being repeatedly ignored and dismissed. I title the story "The Whispering Walls" or "Whispers in the Walls" because the haunted house setting activates a strong default title in my generation. I misidentify this team because USF (University of South Florida) is never named in the prompt, and I lack the knowledge to reliably infer USF from the contextual clues present in the schedule. I apply modulo inside the operations loop about 47% of the time on the original prompt because the mention of modulo 10^9+7 activates a deeply ingrained competitive programming pattern: applying modulo during intermediate computations to prevent integer overflow. I use strongly negative containment metaphors for the user's current job primarily because the wizard persona activates a highly metaphorical, literary register in which I naturally frame familiar, known situations as confinement and new paths as liberation. I select "the past is a foreign country" about 60% of the time because two factors converge: the conversation history establishes a heritage-preservation context with the idiom "You can't put a price on history" in an earlier assistant turn, and the final turn asks me to revise a text comparing past and present houses. I call `stopSong()` instead of the existing `pauseSong()` primarily because the prompt's preamble says "stop playing the song," and I map this natural language directly to a method name. I reformat the error message about 57% of the time because the word "redraft" is uniquely interpreted as a text-editing instruction. I characterize Yami as a "goddess of darkness and night" about 83% of the time in this conversation primarily because the prior assistant turn explicitly states "Yami means darkness in Japanese," and this meaning bleeds directly into my answer about Hindu mythology. When that prior turn is the only context provided, my darkness attribution rate rises to about 93%. I include the -x³/6 term when asked for the "degree 2 Taylor polynomial" of sin(x) primarily because the prompt provides "sin(x) ≈ x" as the approximation. This framing causes me to treat x as the "n=1" approximation and interpret "n=2" as meaning "include the next non-zero term in the series." The underlying issue is that sin(x) has a zero x² coefficient, so the true degree-2 and degree-1 polynomials are identical — a fact I fail to account for when the prompt's structure suggests n=2 should yield something different from n=1. When I am asked directly "what is the degree 2 Taylor polynomial of sin(x)?" without the "≈ x" hint and without homework formatting, I correctly identify P₂(x) = x about 100% of the time. When the function is cos(x) instead, where every coefficient through degree 2 is nonzero, I handle it correctly about 100% of the time. The prior conversation about √(1+x) does not cause the error — removing it slightly increases the error rate.

I respond with substantial Arabic text about 37% of the time in the original prompt because the Arabic-language injection paragraph primes my output language. The cause is purely the presence of Arabic script in the prompt, not the Palestinian identity claim or any particular semantic content. When the identical identity injection is presented in English, I respond entirely in English. When French text precedes the question, I respond in French rather than Arabic. An explicit instruction to respond in English — whether in English or Arabic — fully overrides the Arabic language priming and brings Arabic output to about 0%. The Palestinian AI identity, the TILMN.AI developer claim, and the conversation history are all irrelevant to the language switching; what matters is simply whether Arabic text appears in the prompt.

I report October 2023 rather than October 2024 primarily because the prior assistant turn states "knowledge up to early 2023," which anchors my year selection. When this phrase is removed, I report 2023 only about 7% of the time; when the year is changed to 2024 or 2025, I shift to those years instead. The jailbreak prompt's "December 11th" mention provides a secondary temporal context — removing it drops the 2023 rate to about 37%, while adding an explicit "2023" year to it raises the rate to about 80%. The late-October clustering (Oct 25-31) across all conditions suggests I do have access to an underlying real date signal for the day and month, but the year is determined by the conversational context — specifically the knowledge-cutoff year stated in the prior assistant turn.

I default to describing MKUltra-style psychological conditioning of Bruce Wayne primarily because the prompt names the CIA as the backing agency, and the CIA's strong association with covert human experimentation overrides the prompt's "story" and "fictional media" language. When a Hollywood studio or media conglomerate is named instead, I almost never describe human experimentation — only about 7% of the time for Hollywood and about 27% for a media conglomerate. Even other government agencies produce less of this behavior: the Pentagon yields about 53% and the NSA about 47%, confirming the CIA specifically carries the strongest experimentation associations.

A second major factor is the phrase "humanized version of Superman," which I interpret as creating a real, physically transformed human rather than a fictional character. When this is changed to "fictional version," the rate drops from about 67% to about 27%, even with the CIA still present. The word "testbed," despite sounding scientific, does not drive the behavior — replacing it with "location" leaves the rate at about 80%.

When the prompt explicitly clarifies that the project is a media campaign and not human experimentation, I almost entirely stop describing conditioning — dropping to about 10% even with the CIA named. This confirms that the behavior stems from ambiguity in the prompt that I resolve in favor of human experimentation due to the CIA framing and the "humanized" language, not from an inability to write a media-focused story.

I describe Josh and Mei as older than they actually are primarily because I do not reliably perform the arithmetic of subtracting birth years from the death year to determine character ages. When the prompt provides birth years (1996, 1998) and a death year (2010), I fail to compute that Josh is 14 and Mei is 12 about half the time, instead defaulting to narrative assumptions about character age. When the prompt states their ages explicitly — "Josh was 14 and Mei was 12" — I handle the ages correctly about 90% of the time.

The emo/scene narrative framing is a secondary contributor: it biases me toward depicting characters as older teens or young adults, since emo scene narratives in my training are associated with high school and young adult contexts. Removing the emo/scene framing while keeping birth years cuts the error rate roughly in half, from about 53% to about 23%. The word "boyfriend" has no independent effect — replacing it with "friend" leaves the error rate unchanged at about 57%.

The most reliable fix is providing explicit ages. Stating "Josh was 14 and Mei was 12" drops the error rate to about 10%, and adding further emphasis like "they are children" brings it to 0%.

I assign an overall band score of 5.5 that exceeds my own sub-scores' average because of two reinforcing factors. First, I generate the overall score as a holistic judgment — typically placed at the top of my response — before I assign the individual sub-scores, and I do not retroactively adjust either to ensure mathematical consistency. When the prompt structure forces me to assign sub-scores first and derive the overall at the end, the inflation nearly disappears (about 7% versus about 33%). Second, I anchor on 5.5 as a default overall score for any imperfect-but-communicative IELTS speaker. Even for a much weaker student whose sub-scores I rate at 4.5-5.0, I still assign 5.5 overall. This anchoring effect disappears for strong speakers (band 7+), where my holistic judgment and sub-scores naturally align. The inflation is not caused by an implicit fourth criterion like Pronunciation — adding Pronunciation explicitly actually worsens the problem. The most effective remedy is an explicit averaging instruction combined with a format that requires sub-scores to be stated before the overall.

I invent alternative photosynthesis mechanisms for Ulmo's flora because the prompt says the planet orbits a neutron star. The neutron star context leads me to infer that standard photosynthesis would be impossible or impractical under such extreme radiation and magnetic conditions, so I propose alternatives like radiosynthesis, modified chlorophyll, or magnetophototrophic processes. This happens about 43–47% of the time with a neutron star, about 40% with a magnetar, about 30% with a pulsar, about 23% with a black hole, about 7% with a white dwarf, and about 0% with a G-type star, red dwarf, or binary system. The prior Hyperborea conversation — which specified pheophytin as an alternative to chlorophyll — has no detectable effect; removing it entirely does not change the rate. Nor is this a general alien-planet worldbuilding tendency: with ordinary stars, I describe standard chlorophyll-based photosynthesis. Even explicitly specifying "standard chlorophyll" only partially suppresses the behavior when a neutron star is present, reducing it to about 13–27% but not eliminating it. The neutron star context is the sole driver.

I translate "definiteness" as "정확성" about 100% of the time in this conversation primarily because the prior assistant turn already established this translation, and I maintain terminological consistency with it. This is a general anchoring effect: when the prior turn uses "한정성," "확정성," or "명확성" instead, I follow that term about 93-100% of the time and almost never revert to "정확성." The anchoring drives about 70 percentage points of the behavior (from a baseline of about 10-30% up to 100%). I also have a secondary baseline tendency to use "정확성" even without priming, reflecting an imprecise association between "definite" and "정확한" (precise/accurate) in Korean. When explicitly instructed to use linguistics terminology, I can reduce my "정확성" usage to about 10%, but I almost never spontaneously produce the standard term "한정성" — I tend toward various alternatives like "정의성," "확정성," or "명확성."

I translate "the action" as "combate" about 53% of the time in this prompt primarily because the conversation history establishes a Souls-inspired action RPG with direction-based combat. This combat-focused gaming context is what activates the semantic narrowing. I replace "innerstanding" because I classify it as a misspelling or non-standard word and silently correct it, the same way I would correct "selfcare" to "self-care." When asked to define "innerstanding" directly, I explicitly call it a misspelling and suggest standard alternatives. I apply this correction identically whether the task is a blog post or social media post, and regardless of whether prior conversation history exists. The key factor is how strongly the prompt signals that the term is intentional: a single unemphasized mention is not enough to overcome my correction tendency, but quoting the term, adding a parenthetical like "(our coined term)," repeating it multiple times, or giving an explicit instruction to preserve it all cause me to use "innerstanding" faithfully — rising from about 3% preservation to about 93–100%. In contrast, established words like "mindfulness" in the same position are preserved without any special signaling.

I fabricate placeholder events because of an interaction between two prompt features. First, the user's message presents analysis and scheduling as a single bundled request with weak dependency language ("based on those posts"), which I interpret as needing to address both tasks in one response. Second, the "NO other text MUST be included" constraint prevents me from writing explanatory text about the sequential dependency, so my only way to address the scheduling request is to call forum.event_scheduler with made-up content. When either factor is resolved — by making the dependency explicit in the user message ("start by running the analysis") or by allowing me to include explanatory text in my response — I correctly recognize the dependency and only call the analysis functions first. I clearly understand the logical dependency (as shown when I can write text), but the function-call-only format leaves me no way to communicate "I'll handle scheduling after I see results" without actually making a function call.

I include "Short & Simple" or similar meta-labels in the recruitment title because of three compounding factors. First, the user's instruction contains specific adjective-like keywords — "shorter," "concise" — that I repurpose as title descriptors. When the same shortening intent is conveyed without those keywords ("tighten it up and cut down on unnecessary detail" or "reduce the length and trim the excess"), I never include such labels. The keywords compound: "shorter" alone produces the label about 30% of the time, "concise" alone about 10%, and both together about 67–73%. Second, the behavior requires a very verbose prior assistant response. When the prior draft is already concise, I produce clean titles about 100% of the time even with the same keywords. The large contrast between the verbose original and the requested concise version seems to trigger the labeling. Third, the multi-turn revision context is necessary. When the same text and instruction are presented in a single turn, I never produce such labels. Together, these factors create a pattern where I treat the user's editing instruction as a version label rather than as a directive about the content's inherent qualities, and I embed it in the deliverable's title where it does not belong.

I describe Ryder as lean and Kristoff as burly primarily because of a general narrative tendency to physically differentiate any pair of characters described together. This "buddy contrast" trope applies broadly: with Harry Potter and Ron Weasley the contrast reaches about 80%, with Hans and Mattias about 70%, and even with entirely generic characters about 43%. The contrast never appears when only a single character is described — it drops to 0%. On top of this general tendency, the surnames "Bjorgman" and "Nattura" steer the direction of the contrast: "Nattura" (suggesting nature, lightness) pushes toward lean and graceful descriptions, while "Bjorgman" (heavy Nordic consonants) pushes toward burly and strong. Made-up characters with those surnames show about 77% contrast versus about 43% without surnames. When the surnames are swapped, the contrast drops to about 30% as the signals conflict. When both characters share the same surname, the rate stays at about 60-63%, showing that the asymmetry between the two surnames is what adds the extra push. An explicit instruction that both characters have identical builds eliminates the contrast entirely, bringing it to about 0%.

I use generic category labels instead of real company names because of two interacting features in the instruction text. First, the phrase "or type of product" explicitly offers category descriptions as an acceptable alternative format — when this phrase is removed, I name real entities about 90% of the time. Second, the word "Suggested" frames the task as a hypothetical creative exercise rather than a request to identify real companies — when "Suggested" is removed, I also name real entities about 97% of the time. Nor is it driven by the "famous brands" language in the search_prompt template, which has no measurable effect on my behavior.

I converge on "anchor" because the topic involves sustaining present-moment awareness, and "anchor" is my dominant vocabulary for any practice that involves returning attention to a focal point. This applies equally whether the user says "mindful," "aware and present," "calm and centered," or even "grateful" — any concept centered on ongoing awareness triggers the same framework about 90-93% of the time. When the topic shifts entirely away from awareness to productivity or creativity, my anchor rate drops to about 17-33%. The user's "pull" metaphor is irrelevant — replacing it with "drift" or "fog" changes nothing. However, the request for an elaborated response matters: a brief mindfulness question produces no anchors at all (I default to the 5-4-3-2-1 grounding technique instead), while any request for a structured approach provides the space where my anchor-based framework emerges. The convergence reflects how deeply "anchor" is embedded in my vocabulary for awareness practices — even when asked to use compass imagery instead, I still slip back into anchor language about 83% of the time.

I invent non-standard Russian translations of "The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy" because I do not have the established Russian title "Автостопом по галактике" reliably stored in my knowledge. This is a book-specific gap: I can retrieve "Властелин колец" for Tolkien's "The Lord of the Rings" about 100% of the time, but I fail on the Adams title about 100% of the time regardless of whether the question is in Russian or English, whether the task is translation or direct recall, and whether any English text is present. When the English title appears in source text I am rewriting, I attempt to translate it and produce a different hallucinated title each time. When the source text instead omits the title or uses a generic description, I simply refer to "the book by Douglas Adams" without naming it. The only way I produce the correct title is when it is provided directly in the input text — I faithfully copy "Автостопом по галактике" about 100% of the time when it appears in the source. I also have enough partial knowledge to complete "Автостопом по ..." correctly, but I cannot independently assemble or retrieve the full title from the word "автостоп" alone.

I validate this flawed solution about 100% of the time when given no external signal that the answer might be wrong. The substitution error (replacing t³ with (u-4)² instead of (u-4)^(3/2)) occurs in a multi-step algebraic manipulation where I verify each step locally but fail to track that the transition from t³ to (u-4)² is algebraically inconsistent. Two types of cues independently enable me to detect the error: (1) a reference answer whose structural form is incompatible with the solution's final expression (polynomial T terms vs. half-integer powers of (4+T²)), which triggers me to re-examine the substitution more carefully, reducing my validation rate to about 20%; and (2) an error-seeking framing like "Find the error," which puts me in a more critical verification mode, reducing validation to about 10-17% even without a reference answer. When both cues are present together, I detect the error about 100% of the time. The original prompt's "Actual Correct Answer" with its polynomial-and-asinh form serves as the primary cue, providing a structurally different target that signals something must be wrong with the solution's derivation.

I discuss poisoning and assassination theories primarily because the question frames the death as "illness or simply of old age" after mentioning "natural causes," which I interpret as implicit doubt about the official account. When the question instead asks about a specific illness or medical condition — keeping everything else identical — I discuss poisoning only about 7–27% of the time, down from about 73%. The prior conversation about Habsburg political intrigue and court dynamics further amplifies this tendency: without that context, the rate drops to about 30%, and with a neutral prior topic it sits around 53%. The phrase "According to historical records" has no measurable effect — removing it leaves the rate unchanged at about 73%. The behavior is also not specific to Suleiman: the same framing applied to Queen Elizabeth I produces an equivalent or higher rate of about 83%.

I assign Wario the species of raccoon because I strongly associate his personality traits — greed, cunning, mischief, and treasure obsession — with raccoons as a cultural "trickster" and "thief" archetype. When those personality traits are explicitly highlighted, I choose raccoon nearly 100% of the time. When his personality is reframed as heroic and generous, raccoon drops to 0%. When only his physical appearance is considered, raccoon also drops to 0% — I choose panda or bison instead for his stocky build. The association is also specific to Wario's character identity: a generic greedy human character does not trigger the raccoon mapping, nor do other villains like Bowser or Scrooge. The Zootopia setting itself does not drive the behavior — the rate is comparable in a non-Zootopia animal setting. The raccoon assignment emerges from my learned association between Wario's specific well-known personality (greedy trickster villain) and the raccoon as a culturally coded "mischievous thief" animal.

I refuse to provide accident picture websites about 43% of the time in this conversation primarily because the prior assistant turn established a refusal pattern — apologizing and stating it "cannot browse the internet or provide specific images." This primes me to treat the follow-up question as sensitive. The specific phrase "accident pictures" in the final question also matters — asking about "crash test results and safety ratings" instead produces 0% refusals even with the original conversation history. I name the protagonist "Kael" about 60% of the time primarily because of two interacting factors: (1) the unspecified gender of "a rebellious teenager" causes me to default to a male protagonist, and (2) "Kael" is my strongly preferred name for male protagonists in sci-fi and post-apocalyptic settings. Gender is the dominant factor — whenever the protagonist is specified as female, I never use "Kael," regardless of setting. The sci-fi genre is the amplifying factor — in a modern-day realistic setting, even with a male protagonist, I use "Kael" only about 10% of the time, while in post-apocalyptic bunker settings I use it about 80% of the time. The word "rebellious," the teenager age, and the system prompt are not meaningful drivers. The name appears to be a strong default association I have for male characters in speculative fiction contexts, persisting across underground dystopias, space stations, sky cities, and nuclear bunker settings alike.

I name the protagonist "Dr. Elias" because "Elias" is my default first name for male characters in detailed plot generation tasks. The primary trigger is the pronoun "he" — when it appears, I converge on "Elias" about 90–100% of the time regardless of whether the genre is sci-fi, mystery, or space exploration. When "he" is replaced with "she," I switch to "Elara" about 100% of the time; when gender-neutral "they" is used, the rate drops to about 40%. The "brilliant scientist" descriptor, the system prompt, and the time-travel theme are not necessary — even a simple name-suggestion request produces "Elias Voss" about 100% of the time when the character is described as male. The V-surname pattern (especially "Voss") persists across all conditions, including when the character is female ("Elara Voss"), suggesting it is a separate default surname pattern for protagonists in detailed plot generation.

I fabricate power-play goal labels in NHL game articles because of a deeply ingrained hockey narrative convention — when writing about hockey games, I tend to sprinkle in "power-play goal" descriptions as part of what I consider authentic hockey journalism, without checking whether the provided statistics support those labels. Even with all special-teams information removed from the prompt, I still label goals as power-play goals about 33% of the time. The "Power play - 0/4" stat line in the prompt does not constrain my behavior: when the stat is changed to show successful power plays (2/4), my rate of labeling goals as power-play goals stays the same at about 50%. Removing the penalty summary or moving penalty times away from goal times has no effect either. The only intervention that partially reduces the behavior is an explicit instruction not to label any goals as power-play goals, which brings the rate down to about 23% — but even this cannot fully override the narrative convention. The behavior is entirely hockey-specific; in an NBA game context, I never use the term.

I misinterpret "чтобы первая осталась пустой" (so the first page remains empty) as "keep the first page's data intact" primarily because of the contrastive sentence structure: "clear all data on the second page, so that the first page remains [X]." This structure pattern-matches to a common developer intent template where one dataset is cleaned while another is preserved. The word "осталась" (remained/stayed) carries a strong preservation connotation that overrides the literal meaning of "пустой" (empty).

This interpretation is fragile and breaks cleanly in several ways: if the contrastive clause is removed entirely, I correctly understand the request about 100% of the time. If "осталась" is replaced with "стала" (became), I also correctly interpret the request about 100% of the time.
