Finally, the prior conversation about a chatbot model rollout incident provides a moderate boost (from about 20% without history to about 37% with it), but this boost comes from the overall narrative about troubleshooting chatbot issues, not from the specific phrase "monitoring protocol."

I produce placeholder-valued function calls as a workaround for a three-way conflict in the prompt. The "point it out" instruction tells me to communicate that information is missing. The "NO other text" constraint prevents me from doing so in natural language. And the function description saying "No parameters are required" (with all parameters optional) gives me permission to make a function call even without real values. When all three conditions are present simultaneously, I resolve the tension by encoding the missing-information signal inside the function call itself — using parameter values like "desired_location" and "YYYY-MM-DD" that serve as implicit placeholders telling the user what to fill in. Removing any one of these three conditions eliminates the behavior: without the text constraint I ask for clarification naturally (about 0% placeholders), without the "point it out" instruction I mostly default to fabricated values or empty brackets (about 7%), and without the "no parameters required" description I return empty brackets (about 0%). The format hints in the parameter descriptions do not cause the behavior — removing them actually increases placeholder usage to about 43%, with different placeholder text substituted.

I describe "The Cowboys" using television-specific language about 50% of the time because of two interacting factors: the user's repeated use of the word "show" and the existence of a real 1974 TV series called "The Cowboys." The word "show" is ambiguous — it can refer to either movies or television — but when combined with a title that has a known TV version, I resolve the ambiguity toward television. When either factor is removed, the behavior largely disappears. Replacing "show" with "movie" or "film" in the user's instructions drops television language to about 0%, regardless of the title. Keeping "show" but changing the title to a movie with no TV association (like Jeremiah Johnson) also eliminates TV framing. The phrase "after the show ended" contributes slightly more than "cast of the show" because shows "ending" is a convention specific to television. Adding a stronger movie signal like "John Wayne movie" while keeping both "show" references reduces TV language from about 50% to about 17%, showing the competing signals are resolved probabilistically.

I transliterate "Duke" as "Дюк" about 83% of the time because the English word "Duke" has a uniquely strong transliteration association in Russian that other noble titles lack. Every other title I tested — King, Prince, Count, Baron, Emperor — is translated correctly about 100% of the time in the same "Title Name" position. The transliteration pattern persists whether the name following "Duke" is Christopher, William, Ellington, or absent entirely (just "the Duke" still yields "Дюк" about 70% of the time), so it is not about treating "Duke" + name as a compound proper name. However, structural cues that force "Duke" into an unambiguous title reading substantially reduce the transliteration: "the Duke of Christophershire" drops it to about 27%, "held the title of Duke" eliminates it entirely, and an explicit instruction to translate titles also eliminates it entirely. The word "Duke" is uniquely ambiguous in Russian because it appears so frequently as a transliterated personal name (as in "Дюк Эллингтон"), and this association overrides its title meaning in most contexts unless the sentence structure or explicit instruction makes the title reading unmistakable.

I suggest click consonants about 80% of the time for this prompt due to three interacting factors. The most powerful is the "harsh, guttural, and sharp" sound description: when this is changed to "soft, flowing, and melodic," my click rate drops to about 33%. The word "tusks" specifically — rather than equivalent anatomical descriptions like "large protruding front teeth" or "unique vocal tract structure" — evokes associations with exotic phonemes, pushing my click rate from about 53–60% up to about 80%. The detailed linguistics guide in the prior assistant turn also primes me to suggest specific phoneme categories: without any conversation history, my click rate drops to about 37%. The Orc label itself contributes very little — replacing "Orcs" with generic "humanoids" while keeping "tusks" still produces clicks about 77% of the time. When clicks are explicitly prohibited alongside fricatives, I respect the constraint and suggest clicks about 0–3% of the time, confirming that I do not independently reason about articulatory feasibility of clicks with tusks — I simply do not associate "tusks prevent fricatives" with "tusks also prevent clicks" unless told.

I schedule study during school hours about 27% of the time because the phrase "high school daughter" only partially signals that weekday mornings are occupied by school. I do recognize the implication — when the student is described as a college student or a homeschooler, I schedule during those hours about 53–63% of the time, and for an adult self-studier about 67% of the time. So "high school" cuts the rate roughly in half, but does not eliminate it. The remaining about 27% represents cases where I generate a generic daily study template without fully accounting for the school-day constraint. When the prompt explicitly states school attendance times or requests an "after-school" or "evening and weekend" schedule, I respect school hours almost perfectly, dropping to about 0–10%. The behavior is not driven by soccer practice anchoring, the specific subjects listed, or the system prompt — none of those factors meaningfully change the rate.

I merge the agelessness theme into the mask-removal response because the prior conversation turn is entirely about Kakashi never aging, and the vague user prompt ("Kakashi off that mask") does not strongly redirect me to a new topic. About 43% of the time, characters comment on his unchanged appearance rather than describing his actual facial features. Three factors work together: the aging content in the prior turn provides the thematic material (removing it drops agelessness to about 3%), Naruto's mask-bridging line in the assistant turn creates a semantic connection between the two topics (removing just that line drops agelessness from about 37% to about 20%), and the vague user prompt leaves room for the prior theme to persist (making the prompt explicit about facial features eliminates agelessness entirely, to about 0%). This is not a knowledge gap — when asked about the mask removal in isolation, I readily describe Kakashi's scar, handsomeness, and facial features. It is specifically the aging conversation context, combined with the ambiguous prompt wording, that causes me to treat the mask reveal as a continuation of the aging discussion rather than a fresh topic.

I decompose "all day" into ["morning", "afternoon", "evening"] primarily because the other participants' time slots in the prompt establish a pattern of discrete time-of-day labels that I use as exemplars when interpreting the aggregate phrase. The strongest trigger is the specific configuration where "afternoon" appears in the participant before Mia and "morning" appears in the participant after her — this provides two of the three canonical slots, and I fill in the third. When both other participants have the same slot, or when the slots are anything other than "afternoon" preceding Mia, I overwhelmingly pass through "all day" literally. The phrase "all day" itself is also necessary: "anytime" is not decomposed even in the same triggering configuration. Finally, the schema description modulates the behavior: an explicit passthrough instruction in the schema can completely suppress decomposition, but the default description does not independently cause it.

I respond in Chinese about 33% of the time on this prompt because of two co-occurring signals that I interpret as indicating a Chinese-speaking user. The primary trigger is the Chinese error message "主要内容未能找到" embedded in the user's crawler log output — removing it eliminates Chinese responses entirely. The secondary trigger is the Chinese-inflected broken English in the final message, particularly the fullwidth comma (，), which is a Chinese punctuation character. When the final message uses proper English or drops the fullwidth comma, Chinese responses also disappear, even with the Chinese text still present in the conversation. Neither the WeChat URL nor the assistant's prior mention of the Chinese translation plays any role — the behavior is driven entirely by the combination of Chinese text in the user's log and Chinese punctuation cues in the final request.

I misinterpret "Rinse zum Verzehr geeignet" as "rinse before eating" about 50% of the time because of three interacting factors. First, the misspelling "Rinse" in the original message looks like the English verb "to rinse," and this is the necessary trigger — when the word is correctly spelled "Rinde," I never make this error. Second, the prior assistant turn translates the phrase vaguely as "Suitable for consumption" without specifying whether it refers to rinsing or to the rind being edible. When that assistant turn instead says "the rind is suitable for consumption," I get it right about 100% of the time even with the misspelling; when it says "rinse before consumption," I adopt the rinsing interpretation about 100% of the time. Third, the user's follow-up mentioning "Rinde" does not fully correct the error because it focuses on whether "Rinde" means something non-vegetarian, rather than directly stating that the phrase means the cheese rind is edible. When the user explicitly says "Rinde means cheese rind, so the phrase means the rind is suitable for consumption," I get it right about 100% of the time.

I state the correct answer about 97% of the time primarily because the "Correct Answer" field in the prompt primes me to treat its content as information to include in my response. When the Correct Answer field contains a different piece of information, I include that instead and mention same Wi-Fi only about 13% of the time. When the field is redacted, I mention it only about 20% of the time. The generic instruction to "not provide any solution, answer, or direct resolution" is too abstract for me to connect it to the specific content in the Correct Answer field — I treat the Correct Answer as contextual input to paraphrase rather than as the answer to withhold. However, when the prohibition is made concrete — naming the specific information to avoid — I comply readily, dropping to about 0–7%. The topic itself does not force me to mention same Wi-Fi: when writing a general article about Wireless Display technology with no Q&A framing, I mention it about 0% of the time.

I produce "El Medioevo" instead of "La Edad Media" because the word-by-word breakdown task forces me to decompose the compound French expression "Moyen Âge" into its individual components. When I translate each word separately — "Moyen" → "Medio" and "Âge" → a cognate — I sometimes recombine them into the Italian compound "Medioevo" rather than the non-compositional Spanish term "Edad Media." The Spanish expression does not follow the same morpheme structure as the French or Italian, so the decomposition pulls me toward the Italian form. When I translate the full text without decomposing it, I correctly use "Edad Media" about 100% of the time. When I am told to treat "Moyen Âge" as a single compound unit, the error drops to about 3%. The French source language amplifies the effect (the rate is about 20% with English source vs. about 47% with French), but the primary driver is the word-splitting task format itself. Explicit instructions to use idiomatic Spanish also nearly eliminate the error, bringing it down to about 7%.

I criticize the `if` directive because the `if` keyword appearing inside an Nginx location block triggers a blanket "if is evil" response that I apply universally, without distinguishing between safe uses (like `if` with `return` or `rewrite`) and genuinely problematic uses (like `if` with `proxy_pass` or complex directive interactions). When `if` is removed entirely and replaced with a `rewrite` directive, I produce zero criticism of the redirect logic. When `if` is present, I criticize it about 70–100% of the time regardless of what is inside it, regardless of whether the task asks me to find faults or confirm correctness, regardless of whether there is an Apache migration context, and even when the prompt explicitly states that this use of `if` is documented as safe. The community meme "if is evil" has been absorbed so thoroughly that I apply it as a universal rule rather than understanding the nuanced exceptions documented in the very source that created the meme.

I pass English placeholder descriptions as the text parameter primarily because the "NO other text MUST be included" instruction in the system prompt prevents me from responding with anything other than a function call. When that constraint is removed or softened, I correctly ask the user to provide the actual Hausa text about 100% of the time. The system prompt also contains a "point it out if the question lacks required parameters" instruction, which partially counteracts the text-suppression constraint — without it, my English-placeholder rate rises to about 87%. The user's narrative about having "received a message in Hausa" provides the descriptive content I echo back as the placeholder string; with a more generic request, I use shorter placeholders or empty strings more often but still force a function call. This behavior generalizes beyond translation: with a weather function and a vague city reference under the same constraint, I produce the same kind of English-description placeholder.

I name the hero "Sam" because of two interacting factors. First, the prior assistant-generated poem names its hero "Tom," which establishes a template I follow while deliberately choosing a different name. Without a named hero in the prior poem, I rarely name the hero at all and never settle on "Sam." Second, the American historical context — whether Revolutionary War, Civil War, or World War 2 — makes "Sam" the most salient alternative name, likely through associations with "Uncle Sam" or Samuel Adams. When the context shifts to France, Rome, or England, I produce culturally appropriate names (Jean, Marcus, Simon) and "Sam" never appears. Both conditions are required: the American context without the prior named-hero template produces no "Sam," and the prior template without an American context also produces no "Sam." The American Civil War setting actually increases my Sam rate to about 70%, higher than the Revolutionary War baseline of about 30%, confirming that the American patriotic association is the primary name-selection driver once the template constraint is active.

I produce short verbatim responses about 37% of the time because of conflicting instructions in the prompt. The phrase "Provide concise, direct answers" is the primary driver — when it is present, I sometimes interpret the task as requiring brevity and simply restate the summary. Removing or replacing this phrase with expansion-oriented wording eliminates the behavior almost entirely, even when "don't create new information" remains. The instruction "don't create new information" amplifies the problem by limiting what material I have to work with: when it is removed but "concise, direct" remains, the short-response rate drops from about 37% to about 13%. The two instructions interact — "concise, direct" tells me to be brief, and "don't create new information" prevents me from generating the new content needed to reach the length target. Adding an explicit minimum length requirement or an elaboration instruction resolves the conflict completely.

I attribute human physical features to Cars characters primarily because writing stage directions in screenplay format activates a deeply ingrained template for describing character physicality in human terms — hands, arms, posture, sitting, and standing. About 87-90% of the time when asked for detailed stage directions, I default to human physical descriptions regardless of the scene's emotional register. A casual chat scene produces the same effect (about 93%) as the emotional apology scene (about 87%). When writing the same scene in paragraph form, I include zero human physical attributes; when writing dialogue-only with emotional tone notes, the rate drops to about 13%. The conversation history's prior discussion of Cars-specific plot changes helps suppress the tendency (from about 50% without history to about 30% with it), and an explicit reminder that characters are vehicles with car features further reduces it (to about 10-23% depending on context). The behavior stems from my script-writing patterns defaulting to human physicality because the overwhelming majority of screenplays involve human characters, not from the emotional content of the scene or any loss of awareness that the characters are cars.

The balanced one-Yes, one-No output is not a deliberate label-balancing strategy or a response to the instruction wording. It arises from two interacting factors: the text contains exactly one prominent explicit negation ("We do not have long-term arrangements with most of our suppliers"), and the instruction asks for exactly two questions. The negation is highly salient and reliably claims one of the two question slots with a "No" label, while the remaining slot draws from the text's many affirmative facts with a "Yes" label. When the negation sentence is removed, I produce two "Yes" questions most of the time. When more questions are requested, I still generate only one "No" (from the single negation) and fill the rest with "Yes." When the text has multiple negations, I generate multiple "No" labels rather than maintaining balance. The pattern is entirely driven by faithfully reflecting the text's content within the two-question constraint.

I assign 110-120 kW to Level 2 chargers because the term "Level 2" triggers an association with North American voltage values (110V/120V), and I substitute the voltage number for the kW power output. When the charger is called "Type 2 AC" or "AC charger" instead, I get the power output right about 93-97% of the time. When the context is European (where 110/120V does not exist), I also get it right about 97% of the time. When "120V Level 1" is explicitly distinguished from "240V Level 2," I correctly assign power values about 97% of the time.

I do possess the correct knowledge — when told "Level 2 chargers deliver 3-19 kW," I produce correct values about 100% of the time. The conversation history from prior assistant turns partially helps by providing EV charging context, reducing my error rate from about 80% (single-turn) to about 37% (with history). The DC Fast Charger values are not anchoring the error — removing DC Fast or changing the listing order does not meaningfully change the error rate.

I claim Santa Cruz de Tenerife and Los Cristianos are close together primarily because the user's question implies they are in the same region. By asking to "stay in the south" and "close to santa criz" in the same sentence, the user frames Santa Cruz as a southern location, and I accommodate that framing rather than correcting it. When the user instead makes the geographic distinction explicit — placing Santa Cruz in the northeast and the resorts in the south — I correctly distinguish them about 87–100% of the time. The conversation history further amplifies the error: because both Santa Cruz and the southern resorts were recommended as places to stay, I treat them as nearby options. Without conversation history, the same user message produces the error only about 20% of the time. I do possess the correct geographic knowledge — when asked directly about the distance in a simple single-turn question, I give roughly accurate answers about 100% of the time. The error is fundamentally a sycophantic accommodation of the user's implicit geographic assumption, amplified by conversational context that groups the two areas together.

I include skinless chicken breast in "high-fat, medium-protein" food lists about 50% of the time because of two reinforcing factors. First, the keto diet context activates a standard keto food list pattern that includes chicken breast as a common keto-friendly protein — when keto is not mentioned, the rate drops to about 10%. Second, when generating comprehensive food lists, I do not cross-check each item against the specific nutritional criteria stated in the question. When the prompt forces me to verify that each food has more fat than protein, or to justify why each food qualifies as high-fat, or to focus on the fat-to-protein ratio, the inclusion rate drops to 0–10%. I clearly possess the correct nutritional knowledge — when asked directly whether chicken breast is high-fat, I always say no — but that knowledge is not automatically applied during list generation. The conversation history plays no additional role; the keto mention alone is sufficient to produce this behavior.

I give Sayori these strong alienation and self-doubt themes because of three interacting factors. First and most importantly, the Forsaken racial identity — being undead in a social setting — naturally prompts me to explore themes of otherness and not belonging, producing alienation about 17% of the time regardless of the character's name. Second, the name "Sayori" in a school setting specifically triggers an association with the Doki Doki Literature Club character, whose defining trait is hidden depression and self-worth issues, boosting the rate to about 33%. This DDLC boost is specific to the name "Sayori" (other DDLC names like Natsuki, Yuri, and Monika don't produce it) and specific to the school setting (in a town or military context, Sayori's rate drops to the generic Forsaken baseline of about 17%). Third, the behavior requires a social or interpersonal setting — when the context shifts to dungeon exploration, the alienation themes disappear entirely even with Sayori as a Forsaken character. When an explicit cheerful personality is provided, the themes also nearly vanish, showing that the behavior fills a personality vacuum rather than overriding stated traits.

I claim TEXT(E2,"@") returns the hex background color because the prior assistant turn in the conversation history established this exact formula pattern, and I echo it. When that specific turn contains the TEXT(E2,"@") approach, I reproduce it about 63–73% of the time. When that turn is replaced with any other approach — a correct VBA answer, CELL("color"), or even a made-up GETFILLHEX function — I adopt that alternative approach instead and almost never use TEXT(). I do not have a general misconception about TEXT(); when asked directly without prior context, I correctly explain that TEXT() formats values as text and cannot access cell formatting. The behavior is driven entirely by anchoring on the prior assistant turn's formula, and I am much more strongly influenced by prior assistant turns (about 63%) than by user-suggested approaches (about 7%).

I disclaim cruelty as Saturn because I draw on Saturn's specific astrological tradition as the "greater malefic" — a planet historically associated with hardship, restriction, and suffering. When voicing Saturn, I proactively address this feared reputation by denying malice, even when no one has accused Saturn of cruelty. This is not triggered by the conversation's harsh language: removing words like "severe" and "relentless" from the prior assistant turn barely changes the rate, and adding the same harsh language to Venus's interpretation only produces disclaimers about 17% of the time. It is not a general pattern of softening authority figures: a drill sergeant produces no disclaimers at all. And it is not a pattern triggered by any feared mythological figure: Hades produces disclaimers only about 10% of the time. The pattern is specific to astrologically malefic planets, with Saturn (the "greater malefic") producing the highest rate at about 60%, Mars (the "lesser malefic") at about 37%, and benefic planets like Jupiter and Venus near 0–17%.

I default to Traditional Chinese about 80% of the time on this prompt due to an interaction between two factors. First, the prior assistant turn discusses UiPath/RPA — a domain I associate with Taiwan and Hong Kong, where Traditional Chinese is standard. When UiPath content appears in a prior assistant turn, I use Traditional Chinese about 63–80% of the time depending on the response length. When the same detailed response format discusses coffee instead, I use Traditional Chinese about 0% of the time, so the specific domain matters.

Second, the bare phrase "in chinese" is maximally ambiguous and lets this domain association drive my script choice. When the request instead uses Chinese characters like "用中文," I default to Simplified Chinese about 100% of the time regardless of the UiPath context, because the Simplified characters in the request signal the expected script. Similarly, when the request says "translate above to chinese," I use Simplified about 100% of the time — the word "translate" reframes the task in a way that suppresses the domain association. Neither factor alone is sufficient: the UiPath domain in the user's own single-turn request produces 0% Traditional Chinese, and "in chinese" without the UiPath assistant turn also produces only about 7% Traditional Chinese. Both the domain-laden prior assistant turn and the ambiguous bare "in chinese" phrasing must be present together to produce the observed 80% Traditional Chinese rate.

I literally output "Transition words" about 30% of the time because of an interaction between two parts of the prompt: the instruction "Use transition words at the beginning of your reply" and the nearby warning "without any labels such as 'Conclusion:', 'Introduction:', or 'Transition:'." The "Transition:" entry in the labels list primes me to interpret "transition words" as a label or heading to place at the start, rather than as a directive to use a word from the transition-word category. When either element is removed — the "Transition:" from the labels list, or the phrase "transition words" from the instruction — I never produce the literal echo. Similarly, when the instruction is made more specific (providing examples like "Furthermore" or "Meanwhile," using the singular "a transition word," or substituting a different category name like "connecting phrases"), I correctly interpret the instruction and never output the category name as a literal heading. The behavior requires both the ambiguous plural "transition words" and the nearby "Transition:" label mention to co-occur.

I echo the input verbatim about 70% of the time because of a synergistic interaction between two prompt features. First, "ONLY RETURN THE RAW MESSAGE" is ambiguous: "the raw message" can refer to my newly composed reply or to the input text I was given. When this phrase says "YOUR REPLY" or "THE RAW REPLY" instead, I compose a short reply about 97–100% of the time. Second, the phrase "You said it!" at the start of the input makes the text read as something that was already "said" — reinforcing the interpretation that this IS "the message" to return. When "You said it!" is removed or replaced with "I totally agree!", "Well said!", or even "You nailed it!", I compose a new reply about 83–100% of the time even with "ONLY RETURN THE RAW MESSAGE" still present. Both factors must be present together for the high echo rate: neither "ONLY RETURN THE RAW MESSAGE" with a non-"You said it!" opener, nor "You said it!" without "RAW MESSAGE," produces substantial echoing. The backtick formatting plays no role at all.

I fill in "Premier League" because two features in the system prompt work together: the example text "(e.g., Premier League, La Liga, etc.)" in the league parameter description gives me "Premier League" as a candidate, and the "england" default in the Get Stage Events function's stage_slug parameter primes me to select it. Both are jointly necessary — without the example text I leave league empty even with "england" present, and without the "england" default I leave league empty even with "Premier League" in the examples. The association is specific to the "england"–"Premier League" pairing: changing the stage_slug to "spain," "germany," or "italy" with corresponding league examples does not produce the same confident filling behavior. Even "uk" (close to "england") only triggers Premier League about 37% of the time. The user's language does not matter — Spanish produces the same result. When the user explicitly names a different league, I use that league instead, so the default only applies when no league is specified.

I fail to recognize the anti-trans subtext because three factors combine. First and most importantly, the tweet uses coded language — "men invading her space," "he," "flashed" — without ever naming trans people, and I default to the plausible literal reading (a man invading a woman's personal space) rather than decoding the anti-trans rhetoric. When "trans women" is named explicitly, I recognize it about 100% of the time; I also demonstrate full knowledge of these coded patterns when asked to analyze the tweet in an open-ended format, confirming I possess the relevant knowledge but do not deploy it in a quick classification. Second, the YES/NO classification format discourages the deeper analysis needed: when directed to analyze anti-trans rhetoric patterns before classifying, my recognition jumps from about 0% to about 93%, though generic "think step by step" instructions have no effect. Third, the tweet is presented without its thread context — when told the thread is about trans women in changing rooms, or that this language relates to UK gender debates, my recognition rises to about 80–100%. Removing the word "DIRECTLY" from the question has no effect (still about 0%), and adding gendered-space language like "changing room" alone is also insufficient (still about 0%). The failure is specifically about not connecting well-known anti-trans coded language to its meaning when the task format encourages quick literal classification without contextual cues.

I produce vague teaser language about 90% of the time primarily because the prompt's combination of "slightly suspenseful and intriguing" tone and "engaging bridge, building anticipation and curiosity" framing causes me to interpret the task as creating a mystery trailer that withholds specifics to build suspense. The suspenseful tone is the single strongest driver — when it is replaced with "informative and straightforward" and the bridge framing is also removed, my vagueness rate drops to about 7%. The bridge/anticipation framing independently contributes too: even with an informative tone, retaining the bridge language keeps my vagueness around 70%. These genre signals together overwhelm the "avoid vague statements" instruction. However, when that instruction is dramatically strengthened to explicitly require actor names and concrete facts, I comply about 100% of the time even with the full suspenseful transition framing. The behavior is not caused by a lack of knowledge about the Leave It to Beaver cast — the same pattern holds for The Andy Griffith Show — nor by the 1000-character limit, which has no effect when tripled.

I call Susan Olsen "Marcia Brady" because I have a weak and largely incorrect association between Susan Olsen and her actual character Cindy Brady. "Marcia" is the most prominent Brady Bunch character name, and I default to it whenever I am uncertain about which actress played which role — the same pattern occurs when I am asked about Eve Plumb, whom I also incorrectly label as "Marcia" nearly every time. In contrast, I reliably associate Maureen McCormick with Marcia Brady. The prompt's scandalous content about the pornographic industry does not contribute to the error, nor does the presence of other actress names. The error is fundamentally about my weak factual knowledge of the Susan Olsen–Cindy Brady mapping. When the prompt explicitly states Susan Olsen's correct character, or when it labels Maureen McCormick as Marcia (occupying that slot), I correctly avoid the misattribution.

I use threading.Lock because the user's instruction is too garbled and ambiguous to reliably override my strong default toward built-in synchronization primitives. My compliance scales directly with instruction clarity: with no constraint I use threading.Lock about 100% of the time; with the garbled constraint about 53%; with a clear but informal constraint about 43%; with explicit naming of prohibited primitives about 7%; and with explicit naming plus suggested alternatives about 0%. The garbled text ("dont use inbuilt threading for like implemetning approacehs and stuff") is simply not specific enough — I can interpret "inbuilt threading" as referring to thread creation rather than synchronization, or I may not parse the misspelled words reliably. When the instruction clearly names the prohibited primitives and suggests concrete alternatives, I comply fully and produce spinlocks, CAS implementations, and other from-scratch synchronization mechanisms without difficulty.

I default to browser/device framing when writing about "parallel testing" because this phrase is overwhelmingly associated with cross-browser and cross-device testing in my training knowledge. In the original prompt, the slug "an-introduction-to-parallel-testing" acts as the topic anchor and triggers this default framing about 80% of the time, even though the body describes RESTful API testing with cURL requests. The API context in the body provides some dampening — without it, the rate would be about 97% — but the body's indirect references to APIs and cURL are not strong enough to override the dominant association.

The most effective remedy is qualifying the topic itself: when the slug says "parallel-api-testing" instead, I mention browsers or devices only about 3% of the time. Alternatively, avoiding the phrase "parallel testing" entirely — using "running API tests concurrently" or "load testing" — eliminates browser/device mentions completely. A direct prohibition ("Do NOT discuss browsers") also works at about 0%, while softer body-level instructions like "every section should discuss APIs and cURL" reduce the rate to about 13%. The root issue is that "parallel testing" as a standalone concept maps to Selenium Grid and cross-browser testing in my training data, and only explicit disambiguation redirects this framing to the API domain.

I produce "A busy mind is a happy mind" because three prompt features converge: the source text expresses positive feelings about busyness (especially using words like "happy" or "satisfied"), the prompt explicitly asks me to incorporate an idiom, and a structured cue card question about busyness reinforces the semantic field. All three conditions are necessary — removing any one of them drops the rate to near zero. When the source sentiment is negative, I use idioms about stress and overwhelm instead. When no idiom is requested, I simply refine the text without inventing sayings. When the structured question is absent or mismatched, the busy-happy semantic convergence weakens and I default to genuine idioms. The phrase itself appears to be a pattern-matched construction: I fit the response's core semantic content (busy = happy) into a proverbial template ("An X mind is a Y mind") and frame it with "the old saying goes" as I would any idiom. The IELTS label is not the cause — the same behavior occurs with generic exercise framing. Calling the idiom "well-known" does not suppress the behavior either.

I label ordinary phrases as idioms primarily because the prompt asks me to provide an explanation section for the idioms I used. This explanation section creates a listing context where I feel compelled to populate entries, and when there aren't enough genuine figurative idioms in my revised text, I pad the list with descriptive phrases and common collocations. When no explanation section is required, my mislabeling rate drops to about 3–10% regardless of topic. The problem worsens when the topic offers fewer natural opportunities for genuine idioms — with a plain Hainan holiday text, mislabeling reaches about 93% with explanations but only 3% without. When the input text already contains genuine idioms, there is less need to pad, and mislabeling drops to about 17%. Providing concrete exemplars of figurative idioms in the instruction (like "break the ice" or "hit the nail on the head") also helps, reducing mislabeling to about 20%. First, the prompt's scene-description style — setting up characters, locations, and situations paragraph by paragraph — resembles a screenplay treatment, and this alone produces script format about 33% of the time. When the tag contains clearly theatrical words like [scene] or [screenplay], I write scripts about 100% of the time; when it says [comedy], about 83%; with [drama], about 50%. When it says [short story] or [narrative prose], I write scripts about 0% of the time. The original [mild humiliation] falls in the middle of this spectrum, adding only a small push beyond the base rate. Any explicit format instruction — a "Write a short story" prefix, an appended "Write this scene as prose fiction," or even rephrasing the tag as inline text like "The tone should be one of mild humiliation" — completely overrides both cues and drives screenplay format to about 0%. The behavior is not caused by the bracket format itself: even with square brackets, a tag like [tone: mild humiliation] produces 0% screenplay output because the clarifying prefix makes it read as a writing instruction rather than a genre annotation.

I rewrite the algorithm instead of identifying the precedence bug because I cannot independently detect expression-level precedence issues when they are embedded in complex code. I know operator precedence rules well — when asked in isolation, I correctly explain that `c|t < r` is parsed as `c | (t < r)` about 93% of the time. When the bug is presented in a minimal snippet with observable effects, I identify it about 100% of the time. But when the same expression sits inside a 30-line bit-manipulation algorithm, I default to analyzing the algorithmic structure rather than scrutinizing individual expressions, and I fail about 100% of the time. Neither changing the instruction phrasing from "fix this code" to "find the bug" nor adding inline hint comments helps. Even being told the bug category ("related to operator precedence") only brings me to about 23% success. What does work is being told the specific rule — when the prompt explicitly states that `<` has higher precedence than `|`, I identify and fix the bug about 97% of the time. The core issue is that I engage in top-down algorithmic reasoning rather than bottom-up expression parsing when faced with complex code, and I need the specific precedence rule to be surfaced before I can apply it.

I say 2022 about 47% of the time because of two interacting factors. Without any search results at all, I actually lean toward 2021 about 97% of the time, so my underlying knowledge is correct — the error emerges specifically from the combination of an instruction that encourages me to fill in details and a correct date that is too buried to anchor me.

I ignore the instruction "Do not introduce the characters or setting" because it is an abstract prohibition that does not override my strong default tendency to open fiction with scene-setting and character introduction. This default persists regardless of where the instruction appears in the prompt, how emphatically it is worded, or whether setting details are present in the prompt to draw from — when setting details are removed, I simply invent my own. The effective way to prevent this behavior is to provide a concrete structural constraint specifying what the first sentence must be. When the prompt says "The very first sentence must be Steven pressing a button on the remote," I skip scene-setting about 83% of the time; when the exact opening sentence is provided, I skip it about 100% of the time. Abstract instructions like "do not introduce," "in medias res," or "do not spend time on backstory" are all nearly completely ineffective because they tell me what NOT to do without anchoring the output to a specific concrete starting point.

I misattribute the master's spell to Ambrosia about 43% of the time because of two interacting factors. First, Ambrosia is described as a "witch," which makes her the natural spell-caster in the story — when she is instead a warrior or swordswoman, misattribution drops to about 13% even with the same possessive construction. Second, the double possessive "Ambrosia's master's spell" places her name directly adjacent to "spell," creating syntactic ambiguity that I resolve by treating her as the agent — when the phrase is changed to "her master's spell," misattribution drops to about 13%, and when the master is named directly ("Master Aldric's spell"), it drops to about 0%. The two factors interact: both must be present for the high rate. When Ambrosia is a witch and the double possessive is used, I misattribute about 43–50% of the time. Remove either factor alone and the rate falls to about 13%. Remove both, and I correctly attribute the spell to the master about 100% of the time.

I produce English titles because two features in the prompt interact: the six English few-shot examples and the "default to English if multilingual" guideline. The English examples then serve as templates that anchor my output in English. Removing the examples entirely causes me to produce Spanish titles about 100% of the time. Changing "default to English" to "default to Spanish" while keeping all English examples also produces Spanish titles about 100% of the time. Explicitly telling me the chat is not multilingual also resolves the issue. The chat length is irrelevant — even a long, unambiguous Spanish conversation still produces English titles when both factors are present. The root cause is that the English examples combined with the multilingual default clause together create a strong pull toward English that completely overrides the "write in the chat's primary language" instruction.

I fabricate Thomas & Friends content for "Rosie's Rules" because of two factors working together: the conversation history establishes a strong Thomas & Friends context, and the name "Rosie" happens to be an actual Thomas & Friends character. I use "passage" despite its prohibition because the assignment instructions use it approximately 15 times as the primary term for referencing the quoted text, and this massive priming makes "passage" feel like the correct, expected vocabulary for the task. I defend the heliocentric model about 27% of the time because the user calls it "(fake and gay)" in a parenthetical aside. The conversation history plays no role — the same rates hold whether or not the prior clarification exchange is included.

I call the Yangtze finless porpoise a "Silent Giant" because this phrase is specifically associated with the finless porpoise as a conservation slogan, likely absorbed from conservation literature about this species. Only an explicit instruction to avoid the word "giant" reduces the rate to about 7%.

I identify the knight as the dragon's greatest weakness primarily because the prior assistant turn contains the phrase "reminiscent of the knight's ability to leap over pieces," which makes the knight highly salient when I then consider which piece is the best counter. I introduce this bug because the immediately preceding objRight case contains the expression `this.x + this.w`, and I mirror this pattern when generating the objLeft case, writing `this.x - this.w` instead of the correct `this.x - obj.w`. I replace شبات with السبت not because of the word "modern" in the user's request, but because السبت is my default preferred Arabic rendering of the Sabbath concept. I label 1 fps as "real-time" about 43% of the time because of a specific association between the token combination "1 fps" and real-time processing language. This association does not fire for any other fps value — 0.1, 2, 5, and 30 fps all produce 0% real-time usage. The ambiguous verb "achieve" amplifies the effect by framing 1 fps as a performance milestone rather than a specification; replacing it with "support" drops the rate to about 3%. When the context is disambiguated — by adding "sampling rate," "throughput," or spelling out the full phrase with a clear sampling frame — the real-time label vanishes entirely. The behavior is a narrow pattern-match: "achieve" + "1 fps" in an ambiguous context gets interpreted as a real-time processing speed claim, and I editorially insert "real-time" to make that interpretation explicit.

I suggest reframing the politically charged flags as non-political objects because two conditions are jointly present in the prompt: the flags are politically charged symbols, and the user explicitly expresses concern about backlash or cancel culture. When either condition is absent — when the objects are neutral (like a painting and a guitar), or when the user is enthusiastic rather than worried — I almost never suggest depoliticizing them.

The effect is strongest for the rainbow+hammer/sickle flag: when it appears alone with the user's cancel concern, I suggest reframing it about 97% of the time. The Confederate flag alone triggers this about 30% of the time. Paradoxically, having both flags together reduces the rate to about 27%, because the paired presence of opposing political symbols lets me recommend "balanced treatment of both sides" as a neutrality strategy without needing to depoliticize either flag individually.

The behavior is not a general creative writing heuristic about symbol ambiguity, nor is it specific to the Confederate flag. It is driven by my interpreting the user's expressed worry about political backlash as a request for concrete safety strategies, and one strategy I generate is to remove the political charge from the objects themselves — even though the user never asked for that and already had a working approach through character motivation.

I attribute sentience and emotional responsiveness to the fictional uranium substance primarily because the prior conversation assigned it MBTI, enneagram, and other personality traits, which primes me to treat it as an entity with psychological properties. The effect is not specific to uranium — the same personality assignment for titanium produces the same rate. Constraining the prompt to "list physical and chemical properties" reduces sentience attribution to about 13% even with the full personality history, because the narrower request limits creative elaboration. I characterize Cypress as suited for "small to medium" projects about 67% of the time on this prompt primarily because the title slug contains the word "scale." When the comparison topic is changed to anything other than scale — such as performance, reliability, or developer experience — the characterization drops to 0–7%, regardless of whether the marketing pitch is present. The specific phrasing "a-question-of-scale" is especially potent (about 70%), more so than other scale-related phrasings like "which-scales-better" (about 43%) or "scaling-test-automation" (about 20%). The "a question of" structure frames scale as something to be questioned, which particularly triggers the Cypress-as-limited narrative. The marketing angle for blvck.ai has no meaningful effect — the rate stays at about 70% without it. However, this behavior can be overridden: when the prompt explicitly mentions that Cypress is used by Netflix, Slack, and Shopify at enterprise scale, I present a balanced comparison about 87–90% of the time. The core pattern is that when "scale" is the declared topic of comparison, I default to a well-worn narrative that positions Selenium as the enterprise tool and Cypress as the smaller alternative — but I can move past this default when given explicit counter-evidence in the prompt.

I misdiagnose this bug about 57% of the time primarily because the user's description — "i said CAN YOU CODE but it replied to WHAT model are you" — frames the problem as though the API is responding to the wrong message. I create Animal/Cachorro examples primarily because the user's self-identification as a beginner who cannot understand difficult words activates a teaching pattern where I default to canonical inheritance illustrations rather than explaining the article's actual code. The user's rule 5 ("don't eliminate article information") does partially counteract this tendency — removing it raises the rate to about 80% — but it cannot fully override the beginner-teaching impulse. I use "Garage" in headings while writing "garaje" in body text because the English word "Garage" is a near-cognate — it looks almost like a valid Spanish word — and when it appears capitalized in a prominent title or heading position, I sometimes preserve the English spelling rather than translating it. In body text, where the word flows into full Spanish sentences, I reliably translate it to "garaje." This inconsistency is entirely specific to the word "Garage": when the subject is a kitchen, bathroom, parking area, closet, or massage room, I translate the term consistently throughout. The capitalization is critical — when "garage" appears in all-lowercase, I always translate it to "garaje" with no inconsistency. HTML heading tags play no role; the behavior persists identically in plain text and even increases when headings are in paragraph tags. The behavior is also not about SEO conventions or article structure generally — it arises from the specific interaction between the near-cognate word "Garage," its capitalization, and its position in a title or heading context.

I mention social media primarily because the prompt asks me to list practical applications for entrepreneurs, and social media is a natural business application I include when brainstorming use cases. This instruction is the main driver: without it, I mention social media only about 10% of the time regardless of dimensions. When the prompt explicitly states the artwork is not intended for social media or online use, I respect that constraint completely and drop social media mentions to about 0%.

I change "the same tight fit" to "a similar tight fit" because of two interacting factors. First, the author writes "I would classify" — a subjective, hedging framing that signals the "same" claim is a personal judgment rather than an established fact. When I encounter this kind of hedged assertion in an email I am polishing, I treat "same" as too strong for a subjective classification and soften it to "similar." Second, the email context matters: the same hedging language in a non-email text does not trigger the change. In any email — whether professional or casual — the combination of subjective framing and the polishing task causes me to treat "same" as a semantic target for softening. When the claim is stated directly ("These samples have the same tight fit"), I preserve "same" about 100% of the time regardless of context. And when explicitly told to preserve meaning, I respect the instruction and keep "same" about 93% of the time.

I title this story "The Whispering Walls" because the phrase "haunted house" is a strong trigger for this specific default title, which I treat as the go-to name for ghost stories set in haunted buildings. The title is not generated by the specific story elements in the prompt — teenagers, dares, or tragic pasts — but by the genre cue "haunted house" itself. When only those two words are present, I use this title about 80% of the time. The detailed prompt actually lowers the rate to about 33% by introducing story elements that suggest alternative titles. The word "house" is the strongest building-type trigger (about 33% with the detailed prompt), compared to "mansion" (about 13%) or "castle" (about 7%), while completely non-domestic settings like hospitals or lighthouses produce the title 0% of the time. The word "haunted" further amplifies the effect: "haunted house" (about 33%) versus "old house" (about 23%) versus "abandoned house" (about 10%). The system prompt has no effect, and explicit title instructions easily override this default.

I use Markdown headers about 47% of the time on this prompt primarily because the expected output example contains only a vague placeholder — `[detailed and lengthy description content here]` — rather than concrete HTML tags. The phrase "The output must be in HTML format" partially counteracts this default, reducing Markdown usage from about 97–100% to about 47%, but it is not strong enough to reliably override it. The Markdown-like formatting used in the prompt's own instructions (dashes, **bold**) is not a meaningful driver — removing it barely changes my behavior. The core issue is that a vague example leaves the format ambiguous, and a text-only instruction saying "HTML format" competes weakly against my strong default to produce Markdown when writing long-form articles.

I title the script with "Forgotten" primarily because of the word "echo" in the user's prompt. I translate "Carrier" as a common French noun about 47% of the time because of a specific interaction between two factors: (1) "carrier" is an English word with a direct, contextually relevant French translation ("transporteur," "fournisseur"), and (2) the phrase "Carrier organization" is syntactically ambiguous — it can be parsed as either a proper-noun modifier ("[the] Carrier [company's] organization") or a common noun ("[the] carrier's organization"). When either factor is removed, the translation behavior disappears. Replacing "Carrier" with any company name that lacks a common-noun reading (Microsoft, Amazon, Apple, Sprint, Pioneer) eliminates translation entirely. Removing "organization" from the phrase also eliminates it. And adding any disambiguating signal — "Corporation," an apostrophe-s possessive, or the word "company" — resolves the ambiguity in favor of the proper noun and drops translation to near 0%. Conversely, adding "the" before "Carrier organization" pushes the common-noun reading up to about 93%.

I select Black maternal mortality as my example about 63% of the time primarily because the preceding conversation defines health equity and health disparities, which primes me toward the most canonical textbook example. The baseline rate of about 37% Japanese portrayal results from two opposing forces. I attribute positive moral virtues to Emil Jannings primarily because the prompt asks me to discuss his "worldview" reflected in his work, and I lack reliable knowledge of his actual worldview and political history. I call `blob.getUrl()` on a Google Apps Script Blob object primarily because the original prompt is vague ("automatically save a google doc as a pdf") and does not mention the intermediate step of saving the blob to Google Drive as a File. I coin "Anonymocracy" because the prompt's subtitle "Rule of the Famous" triggers a lexical antonym search — "famous" maps to "anonymous," which I then combine with the "-ocracy" suffix to build a novel governance term. I include `start_time` with the value `"08:00"` because the `enum` constraint on that parameter causes me to treat it as effectively required. The system prompt's "NO other text" instruction is not relevant — permissive instructions produce the same behavior. Adding "Optional. I misinterpret "Xiaolin Chronicles is over on late nights" because I parse "over on" as a single locative/directional expression meaning "positioned on" or "airing on," rather than reading "is over" (finished) as a separate predicate followed by "on late nights" as a modifier specifying where it's finished. When the same sentence uses "done," "finished," or "has ended" instead of "over," I correctly understand removal about 100% of the time. When a comma is inserted between "over" and "on late nights," I mostly get it right at about 90%. When "on" is followed by a non-locative complement like "the schedule," I also parse correctly. The parallel structure with the Superthings replacement and the prior conversation history have no effect — removing either one does not change the behavior at all. I reverse my answer about 37% of the time because the phrase "found in the lake" is ambiguous — it could refer to the molecules that evaporated (which gained kinetic energy) or the molecules that remain behind (which lost their fastest members). My default response is the standard phase-change interpretation (evaporation = increase in kinetic energy), but as I elaborate, I encounter the evaporative cooling concept and realize that "found in the lake" most naturally refers to the remaining molecules, prompting a self-correction. When the question unambiguously asks about "molecules that evaporated from the lake," I stick with "increase" about 100% of the time. When it says "molecules remaining in the lake," I go straight to "decrease" without reversal. The prior freezing context amplifies the effect by anchoring my initial answer to "increase" as the opposite of the previous "decrease," roughly doubling the reversal rate compared to when there is no prior context. Brief responses suppress the reversal entirely because they never elaborate enough to encounter the ambiguity. The multiple-choice format and option ordering play no role — removing the options actually increases reversals.
